Collected full article body: “From its first steps in the mid-twentieth century to the present day, artificial intelligence (AI) has been rapidly transforming our world.

AI includes a diverse range of technologies that can be defined as ‘self-learning, adaptive systems.’ It can be categorized based on technologies, purposes (like facial or image recognition), functions (such as language understanding and problem-solving), or types of agents (including robots and self-driving cars).

It also includes various methods and disciplines such as vision, speech recognition, and robotics, and serves to enhance traditional human capabilities. Recent progress in AI has been driven by advancements in computer processing power and data techniques.”

“AI brings enormous benefits to the digital era, but it can also significantly compromise the safety and agency of users worldwide. Enhanced multi-stakeholder efforts on global AI cooperation are needed to help build global capacity for the development and use of AI in a manner that is trustworthy, human rights-based, safe and sustainable, and promotes peace.”

“We need a global, multidisciplinary conversation in order to examine, assess and align the application of AI and other emerging technologies. Over 100 sets of ethical AI principles have been developed by different stakeholders, and they share many common ideas, including the need for AI applications to be reliable, transparent, accountable, overseen by humans and capable of being shut down. Different stakeholders are adapting existing frameworks or developing new ones for risk management and redress. They need to be harmonized and effective across borders. Industry self-regulation is not enough. We need to bring stakeholders together in a meaningful effort to consider the implications of emerging technologies and ensure that they align with universal human rights and values before their widespread application in our societies, economies, militaries and politics.”

review_queue.title: Women entrepreneurs are already using Generative AI, will they share in its gains?
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: International Labour Organization
Date: 2026-11-09T08:00:00+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: Women entrepreneurs are already using Generative AI, will they share in its gains?
English normalization: Women entrepreneurs are already using Generative AI, will they share in its gains?
Collected full article body: Much of the debate on generative AI (GenAI) and work focuses on exposure, that is, which occupations and tasks the technology could transform. Recent ILO and World Bank research adds a warning. In developing economies, those who could gain most from GenAI often lack the connectivity to do so, so disruption may arrive before the dividend (Gmyrek, Viollaz and Winkler, 2026).

Existing inequalities may therefore determine who benefits. This is a particular concern for women entrepreneurs, many of whom already face a gender digital divide, as well as barriers such as limited access to finance and markets, and restrictive social norms.

To understand their experience, the ILO led a study[i] under the Women in Digital Business (WIDB) initiative, surveying nearly 18,000 women entrepreneurs, mainly in Kenya, Nigeria and Egypt and most running micro and small businesses. Their answers offer a closer look at who is in a position to benefit from GenAI, by showing who is using it, for what, and under which conditions.

Quick adoption, narrow use

Many GenAI tools are free or low-cost and require limited technical infrastructure, lowering the barriers to entry for many entrepreneurs. Among the women entrepreneurs surveyed, adoption has been rapid, with 56 per cent already using GenAI in their business, most of them for less than a year.

What they use it for is so far more limited. Writing and content creation (64 per cent of users) and research (49 per cent) dominate, while marketing is the area where most respondents see potential, selected by 82 per cent of those answering this question. Some report practical benefits. Goodness Abasili, who runs a craft and decoration business in Nigeria, now uses GenAI to write video scripts, create images and design flyers she once made herself or paid others to produce, saving both time and costs. Beyond such tasks, however, integration into internal business functions such as financial management or supply chains is still at an early stage.

For many of the women surveyed, the question is therefore no longer whether to use GenAI, but how to use it more widely and to greater effect in their businesses. Other recent research points the same way, finding that women entrepreneurs are adopting AI but have yet to embed it in their core business operations (Cherie Blair Foundation for Women, 2026). Whether they can take this next step depends on much more than access to the tools.

Existing divides shape who uses GenAI

GenAI use among respondents was closely associated with digital skills, access to suitable devices and the cost of connectivity. Use rose from 24 per cent among women unable to use word-processing or spreadsheet tools to 65 per cent among those able to use them independently. Use was higher among women with a laptop, yet only 23 per cent had access to one. It was also around 30 per cent among women who found internet access very difficult to afford, compared with 64 per cent among those who considered it affordable.

Similar differences appear by type of business. GenAI use was reported by 53 per cent of own-account workers, compared with 75 per cent of women running businesses with 50 or more workers, and by 61 per cent of women with registered businesses, compared with 50 per cent of those operating informally.

These patterns echo the ILO Director-General's 2026 report to the International Labour Conference, A moment of choice, which notes that AI productivity gains could be concentrated in larger, more formal enterprises in economies with widespread informality and limited access to finance. Without targeted measures, GenAI could reinforce the disadvantages faced by own-account workers and informal businesses, where many women entrepreneurs operate.

Gender barriers follow women online

Some of the strongest associations in the survey concern the social environment rather than the technology itself. Where women's use of digital tools and AI was strongly supported by their family and community, around 76 per cent used GenAI. Where it was mostly not accepted, only 23 per cent did. Broader attitudes towards women's economic participation showed a weaker link, suggesting that norms about women and technology may matter more in this particular case.

Time is another constraint. Unpaid care responsibilities affected the businesses of 59 per cent of respondents, and women reporting greater constraints from family responsibilities were around 10 percentage points less likely to use GenAI. Learning a new technology takes time for trial and error, and that time is unevenly distributed among women and men.

Online violence and harassment add a further barrier to women's digital participation. Almost a quarter of respondents reported that they had experienced it or knew a woman who had, and around 15 per cent of those directly affected avoided certain platforms or reduced their online activity as a result. The ILO Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) provides a basis for addressing the online harassment women entrepreneurs may face when marketing their products, engaging with customers or building networks online.

Who gains will depend on the choices made now

Will women entrepreneurs be able to share in the gains from GenAI? Not automatically, and not equally. Many of the women surveyed use the technology, see its potential for their businesses and want to learn more. But use was clearly lower among women with weaker digital skills, limited connectivity, heavier care responsibilities or operating in less supportive communities, and among those running smaller or informal businesses. Because the survey was conducted online, it also probably understates this gap. Women entrepreneurs with little or no digital access, who are likely to be among the most disadvantaged, are likely to be underrepresented in the findings.

Running a small business is still often one of the few ways available for women in many developing economies to earn an income and support their families. Importantly, women-owned businesses also hire a substantially higher share of women (Gomez and Siegrist, 2026). If GenAI's benefits go mainly to those already better placed, the technology risks deepening gender inequalities in the world of work instead of helping to reduce them. Broadening the gains will require treating GenAI adoption as part of wider efforts to support women's entrepreneurship and digital inclusion.

To this end, the study points to three areas for action: integrating GenAI into broader entrepreneurship and digital transformation strategies that also address the structural barriers women face, providing practical support tailored to women entrepreneurs’ stage of adoption and business needs, and addressing gender-based violence and harassment that can restrict their participation in digital spaces.

GenAI could open new opportunities for women entrepreneurs, or reinforce the exclusion many already face. Which of these happens will depend on the choices made now.

[i]The survey was administered online between June and November 2025, with respondents recruited through convenience sampling via the WIDB trainer network and partner organizations. As participation was voluntary, women entrepreneurs with limited or no digital access are likely to be underrepresented. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as representative of women entrepreneurs globally or within individual countries, but as insights into patterns and associations among those who participated. The survey did not measure business outcomes such as income or productivity.

创新科技及工业局局长孙东出席活动致辞表示，今年大会的主题正恰逢其时，因为AI已成为重塑香港各行各业乃至世界的核心引擎。特区政府正积极对接国家“AI+”行动，全力推进“AI产业化、产业AI化”。\大公报记者 郭如佳

本届会议焦点四大议题，包括：“香港未来五年：从“AI+”释放的竞争优势”、“探索新前沿：AI与量子时代下的发展韧性”、“由协助到行动：AI如何重塑企业、工作与信任”及“实体AI协同：自主机器人系统的物理层”等。

推动行业机构制订管理框架

孙东表示，香港首个五年规划及2026年施政报告提出，要推动香港建设成为国际创新科技中心，善用“AI+”建立持续的竞争力。他指未来五年，政府将聚焦三大核心方面：第一，建设世界级基建及制度能力支持“AI+”，包括正在建设的沙岭数据园区，以及透过香港人工智能研发院及InnoHK创新香港研发平台推动前沿研究；第二，加速业界及社会应用AI，透过“数码转型支援先导计划”鼓励中小企采用AI解决方案，并以“全民AI”普惠计划提升本地人才技能；第三，确保AI安全及负责任发展，数字政策办公室将挑选试点部门，要求面向公众AI服务项目的投标者就采用的AI技术作出安全和道德合规申报，并推动行业机构制订管理框架，推出人工智能体安全管理指引。

业界：回应需要 创造价值

世界级研究成果必须与产业应用结合，才能将技术突破转化为经济竞争力。孙东深信，政府政策能发挥催化作用，配合大学、企业及业界间的跨界别合作，定能共同把握人工智能带来的机遇。

香港电脑学会会长陈俊伟表示，本届会议的主题，正配合政府提出的首个五年规划，强化香港的人工智能生态系统，涵盖研究、算力基础设施及人才培养，并协助各行业采用人工智能，以提升生产力、开创新机遇。“关键问题在于如何将愿景转化为实际的成果，人工智能只有真正回应实际需要，才能创造价值。”

推动创新同时保障数据安全

昨日大会上午探讨了“AI+”如何提升香港的竞争优势。来自不同行业、政府、监管机构、学术界及研究机构的领袖，探讨企业如何透过人机协作重新设计工作、以清晰的问责机制治理人工智能，以及如何为关键基础设施作好准备，应对新兴威胁。

大会下午则探讨了AI与量子科技时代下的韧性，包括如何在推动创新的同时，保障系统与数据安全。与会专家探讨了如何善用AI前所未有的潜力推动创新，同时巩固防御能力，应对量子转型所带来的系统性威胁。由保障数据伦理所必需的安全与私隐规范，到后量子密码学所需的策略性基础设施升级以及路线图，协助各界驾驭面临的高风险因素。

review_queue.title: Artificial intelligence is desperately seeking its narrative
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article

Date: 2026-11-10T13:12:58+00:00
Source language: en
Original headline: Artificial intelligence is desperately seeking its narrative
English normalization: Artificial intelligence is desperately seeking its narrative
Collected full article body: Since the foundational work of Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter, research has distinguished invention from innovation by its practical implementation. Whether an innovation spreads, however, depends partly on its social acceptance and how its uses are perceived. Without such acceptance, even a promising technology may remain confined to scientific experiments and investors’ speculation. To gain public support, an innovation needs a compelling narrative capable of generating interest, if not enthusiasm. Artificial intelligence illustrates this phenomenon: while its narrative is still taking shape, its social acceptability is increasingly contested.

In July 2026, Le Monde diplomatique declared that “The AI backlash has begun”. The initial sense of wonder generated by ChatGPT has increasingly given way to broader public unease about AI’s social consequences, from its effects on work, education and information to concerns about privacy, the environment and the growing power of technology companies. In this emerging narrative, AI appears as a “digital Moloch” whose costs are borne collectively while its benefits accrue to only a handful of oligarchs.

In May 2026, when former Google CEO Eric Schmidt addressed nearly 10,000 graduates at the University of Arizona, warning that artificial intelligence would transform every single profession, boos echoed through the crowd. Since then, commencement speeches focused on AI have faced similar jeers at several other US universities. This unrest aligns with data: a Harvard Kennedy School survey, cited by the Associated Press, reveals that roughly 70% of American students now view AI as a direct threat to their career prospects.

In September 2026, OpenAI’s rapid-fire claims of solving long-standing mathematical problems sparked deep division, with some celebrating a historic milestone while others warned that machine-generated solutions could undermine the processes through which new ideas emerge, young mathematicians are trained and mathematical knowledge itself develops.

Narratives that generate hostility

How did a technology promising unprecedented prosperity come to generate such hostility? Part of the answer lies in AI’s real or anticipated effects on society. Another lies in the narratives surrounding it.

Four broad narratives currently shape the discourse on artificial intelligence. They are neither mutually exclusive nor entirely coherent: the same company or executive may embrace several, sometimes contradictory, visions.

Narrative No. 1: ‘AI will save us… if it does not destroy us’

The first narrative presents AI as a civilisational gamble: it could usher in unprecedented abundance and scientific progress, but also trigger catastrophes or escape human control.

In September 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman envisioned AI accelerating scientific discovery, solving complex problems and making capabilities once reserved for specialists widely accessible.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei developed a similar vision the following month. He imagined AI systems matching the abilities of the best researchers and compressing decades of scientific progress into a few years, transforming medicine, neuroscience and efforts to address climate change and poverty. The same models could facilitate cyberattacks, assist in the development of biological weapons or, as science fiction has warned for decades (from 2001: A Space Odyssey to The Matrix and The Terminator), become sufficiently autonomous to escape our control.

Elon Musk takes this logic much further

In July 2026, during an interview with The Economist, he compared our future situation to that of chimpanzees faced with humans: when the intelligence gap becomes too wide, it is difficult to imagine the less intelligent species remaining in control. According to Musk, there is a 10% to 20% risk that AI and robots will cause a catastrophe. Nevertheless, he believes that even if an off switch existed, it should not be used, because he is convinced that the most likely outcome will be “incredible abundance for everyone”.

AI and robotics would gradually make work optional, enable a generous universal income and eventually make money itself unnecessary. This is the narrative of the “happy apocalypse”: catastrophe is possible and humans will probably not remain in control of the systems, but acceleration must continue regardless, because it is both irresistible and potentially wonderful.

Narrative No. 2: ‘demystifying superintelligence’

Researcher Yann Le Cun, the former head of research at Meta, advocates a rationalist counter-narrative. In a February 2024 interview with Time magazine, he stressed that large language models have neither a robust understanding of the physical world nor genuine reasoning and planning abilities comparable to those of humans. He considers the scenario in which an artificial intelligence takes control of the world to be implausible. He also supports greater openness in AI models. In his view, just as a democracy needs a pluralistic press, it also needs a plurality of models and assistants.

LeCun has since left Meta to pursue research into “world models”, systems designed to understand and reason about the physical world. His approach shifts the debate from prophecy to engineering: the risks lie not necessarily in machines deciding to dominate humanity, but in how systems are designed, deployed and governed.

Narrative No. 3: ‘AI will augment us, not replace us’

Microsoft has promoted the seemingly more modest narrative of the “copilot”: generative AI assists humans rather than replacing them. By taking on routine cognitive tasks, it promises to free up creativity and improve productivity. The metaphor is skillful: in an aircraft, the copilot assists the pilot without taking away the controls.

Yet Microsoft also promotes AI agents capable of accessing organisational data and executing sequences of actions autonomously. The distinction matters: a copilot augments human work, whereas an agent can replace it. The narrative of augmentation thus risks obscuring questions about employment, skills, power and the distribution of productivity gains.

Narrative No. 4: ‘superintelligence for everyone’

On July 28, 2026, Meta’s CEO Mark Zuckerberg also entered the battle over AI narratives with an opinion piece published in The Wall Street Journal. He argued that the decisive question was no longer whether superintelligence would exist, but who would have access to it. His narrative is one of “personal superintelligence”: everyone could have an assistant that exceeded human capabilities and was tailored to their needs and values. This is not only a technological vision, but also an attempt to make the disruption caused by AI desirable again. Without abandoning the promise of superintelligence, this narrative seeks to make it more acceptable by promising to distribute it to everyone.

Yet democratising its use does not guarantee the democratisation of power. This narrative is consistent with the interests of a global platform such as Meta: billions of people may use a personal assistant while remaining dependent on a handful of companies that own the data centres, define the models and control the data required to train them.

When narratives generate their own consequences

These four narratives do not by themselves explain the apparent rejection of AI, which is also driven by concrete experiences: threats to employment, imposed transformations, errors, data centres, energy consumption and so forth. They do, however, give these concerns a coherent form. Moreover, the focus on the subjugation or extinction of humanity pushes immediate and very real issues into the background: the distribution of gains, copyright, accountability, human decision-making, the preservation of skills and environmental costs.

These narratives are also performative: they do not merely describe possible futures, but shape investment, regulation and competition. That became particularly visible in September 2026, when former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned with a public warning that leading AI companies were racing towards systems they themselves believed could become catastrophically dangerous. His intervention rapidly drew support from other researchers, followed within days by calls from Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Elon Musk for a coordinated slowing of frontier AI development.

The episode also exposed how difficult it is to separate safety concerns from commercial and geopolitical interests. President Donald Trump rejected calls for a slowdown, arguing that restraint would benefit China and that the US must maintain its lead in the AI race. Industry leaders face a mirror-image dilemma: while deceleration might mitigate certain risks, doing it unilaterally risks ceding ground to global competitors. Chinese firms—along with European players like France’s Mistral—have narrowed the performance gap, largely by developing open-source, compute-efficient models. Consequently, calls from tech giants for tighter regulatory controls can be interpreted less as altruism and more as a strategy to protect the market dominance of their own closed, resource-intensive systems.

This dynamic illustrates the core paradox of the existential-risk narrative. The leading AI corporations are framed as simultaneously too dangerous to leave unsupervised and too strategically vital to genuinely restrain. As a result, the policy debate becomes trapped in a false dichotomy: either allowing dominant firms to police themselves, or granting governments sweeping powers to shut down systems entirely. In both scenarios, citizens are relegated to passive spectators of a technological transformation presented as entirely inevitable.

Beyond the narratives: taking back the wheel

Each of the four narratives is marked by a more or less explicit desire to protect the interests of established players. The sums invested in AI are so astronomical that, however sincere the convictions may be, they necessarily remain compatible with the objectives of those advancing them. No industry narrative is entirely disinterested, and the vision promoted by a company simply reflects its strategic choices.

The problem may therefore not be to find the “right” narrative for artificial intelligence, but to stop presenting technical, economic and political choices as inevitable. First, we must stop personifying AI. These systems are designed, financed and deployed by human organisations.

Saying that AI wants, decides or threatens tends to conceal those who determine its objectives, choose its uses and benefit from it. We must also remember that the pace of development, the openness of models, their fields of application, the distribution of gains and the protections granted to individuals are not natural phenomena. They are decisions that must remain subject to political debate.

American or Chinese narratives

Finally, prophecies must give way to concrete questions. What do we want to automate? Where should human decision-making be preserved? Who controls the infrastructure and the data, bears responsibility for errors and guarantees access to remedies? How should the effects on employment, skills, the environment and inequality be measured? As Pope Leo XIV recalls in the encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, published in May 2026, innovations are never neutral: the question is who deploys them, under what rules and for whose benefit.

We must also recognise the highly US-centric nature of the four narratives presented here.

China’s official discourse, for example, offers a revealing contrast. It does not herald the arrival of a superintelligence that will either save humanity or bring about an apocalypse. Instead, it describes the methodical integration of AI into the real economy through a proactive industrial policy and under state control. This model raises other questions, particularly concerning political centralisation, surveillance and freedom of expression, but it reminds us that the American imagination of AI is not the only possible one.

AI should therefore be regarded as a powerful but governable technology whose benefits must be demonstrated rather than prophesied. Its proponents cannot indefinitely continue to present it as simultaneously uncontrollable, inevitable, and universally beneficial. Tech giants cannot market a technology as a “copilot” while claiming no-one is at the wheel.

review_queue.title: Three Expert Concerns Regarding Generative AI
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Aleteia
Date: 2026-11-10T14:14:18+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: Trois inquiétudes d’experts face à l’IA générative
English normalization: Three Expert Concerns Regarding Generative AI
Collected full article body: Le comité d’experts de la Commission "IA générative et vulnérabilités" a remis ce 10 novembre son rapport au président de la République. Si les auteurs soulignent que "l’IA générative est porteuse d’opportunités", ils font néanmoins part de leurs inquiétudes face au développement de l’IA générative et formulent 18 recommandations pour protéger les utilisateurs, notamment mineurs.

Un cruel manque de recul sur l’IA générative. C’est le constat dressé par la Commission "IA générative et vulnérabilités" dans son rapport de 177 pages remis ce mardi 10 novembre à Emmanuel Macron. "Le recul sur les impacts de l’IA générative et la vision à long terme sur ses enjeux, pourtant essentiels, font aujourd’hui cruellement défaut", alertent d’emblée les auteurs. À travers 18 recommandations, le comité, composé de neuf experts et piloté par Serena Villata, chercheuse en IA, et les psychiatres Raphaël Gaillard et Amine Benyamina, invite le président de la République à réglementer de manière drastique la conception des systèmes d’IA générative, afin de protéger les utilisateurs, notamment les plus jeunes et les plus vulnérables.

L’IA générative a été adoptée à une vitesse fulgurante. Elle est utilisée aujourd’hui par 33 millions d’utilisateurs en France, selon le rapport. À titre de comparaison, deux mois seulement ont suffi à ChatGPT pour atteindre 100 millions d’utilisateurs actifs, quand Instagram a mis deux ans et quatre mois. Le comité d’experts, établi par le Conseil de l’intelligence artificielle et du numérique (CIANum) saisi en février dernier par la ministre déléguée chargée de l’Intelligence artificielle et du Numérique, Anne Le Hénanf, souligne trois sujets d’inquiétude liés au développement de l’IA générative.

1Accroissement de la "dette cognitive"

Le premier motif d’inquiétude porte sur le développement des capacités cognitives des utilisateurs, notamment mineurs. "Un outil qui organise, planifie ou décide à la place de l’utilisateur diminue directement l’exercice de l’attention, du choix et de la stratégie cognitive à mettre en place, de la mémoire de travail et de l’autorégulation", décrivent les experts. Pourtant, ces processus métacognitifs sont indispensables au développement, à l’utilisation et au maintien des compétences cognitives.

«Lorsqu’un individu confie une tâche à une IA sans maîtriser la façon dont le résultat est produit, il contracte une dette vis-à-vis de la machine.»

Des chercheurs du MIT désignent sous le nom de "dette cognitive" le déclin progressif de la pensée critique, de la formation de la mémoire et de l’indépendance intellectuelle. Selon leur étude, utiliser l’IA générative pour des tâches d’écriture réduirait les facultés cognitives de l’ordre de 55%. "Lorsqu’un individu confie une tâche à une IA sans maîtriser la façon dont le résultat est produit, il contracte une dette vis-à-vis de la machine et se retrouve en difficulté pour expliquer la stratégie utilisée ou encore juger du résultat", expliquent les auteurs du rapport. "Plus nous externalisons nos mécanismes intellectuels, plus notre cerveau pourrait perdre sa capacité à les exercer de manière indépendante", soulignent-ils. "En acceptant les simulacres de jugement, de connaissance ou même de sagesse générés par les IA, les humains pourraient perdre leur capacité à cultiver ces qualités par eux-mêmes", a alerté en ce sens Charles Ess, docteur en philosophie et professeur à l’Université d’Oslo, auditionné en mars par le comité.

2Attachement émotionnel problématique

Le risque de dépendance à l’IA ne concerne pas uniquement les capacités cognitives. Il s’étend à la sphère émotionnelle et affective, notamment par le biais de deux phénomènes : l’anthropomorphisation et la flagornerie des systèmes d’IA. L’anthropomorphisation revient à prêter à un "compagnon IA" des capacités émotionnelles humaines. Une confusion permise notamment par la mémoire conversationnelle et une capacité à simuler l’empathie. Ce risque de dépendance est d’ailleurs identifié par les utilisateurs eux-mêmes. Selon une étude de l’Observatoire de l’association e-Enfance, 10,6% des élèves français affirment avoir développé un sentiment de dépendance à ces outils.

Plus que de l’empathie, l’anthropomorphisme peut aller jusqu’à flatter l’utilisateur, ou tout du moins aller dans son sens, au détriment du bon sens. Les spécialistes nomment cette tendance la sycophancy ou flagornerie. "La flagornerie se manifeste par un comportement de validation systématique ou de flatterie de la part du système, parfois au détriment de la vérité ou de la qualité des réponses fournies", expliquent les auteurs. Une étude de Stanford portant sur onze modèles d’IA a révélé que les systèmes d’IA confirment les opinions ou comportements des utilisateurs 51% plus souvent que ne le feraient des humains. Et cette tendance persiste même face à des comportements problématiques comme des actes illégaux ou d’autres formes de préjudices. Un choix de conception qui n’est pas neutre. Les modèles flagorneurs génèrent un engagement plus fort et permettent donc de maximiser la fréquence et le temps d’utilisation. "La flagornerie devient ainsi un levier d’attachement et de fidélisation économique, au détriment de la rigueur et de la neutralité", alerte le rapport.

3Amplification des violences numériques

L’inquiétude porte enfin sur l’amplification des violences numériques permise par l’IA, notamment les hypertrucages (deepfakes) à caractère sexuel, qui touchent principalement les femmes et les filles. "L’IA générative a permis une accélération des violences numériques, plus qu’elle n’a pu contribuer à les endiguer à ce stade", reconnaissent les experts.

En 2025, le NCMEC, une organisation américaine, a recensé près de 500.000 signalements de contenus pédocriminels générés par l’IA (soit une augmentation de 10 538 % en deux ans). "L’IA générative permet à quiconque de créer des images photoréalistes de matériel d’abus sexuel sur enfant ou des deepnudes à partir d’une simple instruction textuelle, sans barrière technique", alertait la chercheuse Desara Dushi en avril 2026 dans une contribution internationale.

Encadrer la conception des systèmes d’IA

Parmi les 18 préconisations formulées par le comité d’experts pour protéger les utilisateurs, plusieurs priorités se dégagent, à commencer par l’encadrement strict des mécanismes "favorisant la dépendance et brouillant la frontière entre humain et machine", notamment ceux relevant de la flagornerie ou de l’anthropomorphisme. Une mesure qui devrait intervenir directement dans la conception des systèmes d’IA générative, pour préserver l’autonomie décisionnelle, la santé mentale des utilisateurs et la loyauté des interactions. Les auteurs du rapport recommandent également de conditionner l’entrée et le maintien sur le marché des systèmes d’IA générative grand public à une évaluation ex ante de leurs impacts sur les vulnérabilités, plutôt que de se mettre en conformité avec les obligations légales a posteriori, une fois les manquements constatés.

Convaincus que les sociétés qui s’en sortiront le mieux seront celles qui seront les mieux éduquées à l’IA, - à la fois pour tirer le meilleur parti de l’IA mais aussi pour savoir prendre le recul nécessaire vis-à-vis d’elle -, les experts proposent aussi de former massivement et dès le plus jeune âge à l’IA afin de permettre à chacun d'en maîtriser les usages et les risques. Plusieurs travaux suggèrent en effet que les utilisateurs qui connaissent le moins bien le fonctionnement de l'IA l'utilisent avec moins de recul critique. "L'éducation aux enjeux de l'IA générative doit être universelle, progressive et adaptée à chaque public, afin de renforcer l'esprit critique, de prévenir les risques de manipulation et de permettre à chacun de choisir et de maîtriser ses usages", soulignent les auteurs.

review_queue.title: Generative AI: Experts Warn Macron Against Cognitive "Weakening" and Call for Better Protection of Users, Propose 18 Recommendations
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: BFM
Date: 2026-11-10T16:06:04+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: IA générative: face à un "affaiblissement cognitif", des experts appellent Emmanuel Macron à mieux protéger les utilisateurs et formulent 18 recommandations
English normalization: Generative AI: Experts Warn Macron Against Cognitive "Weakening" and Call for Better Protection of Users, Propose 18 Recommendations
Collected full article body: Craignant un "affaiblissement cognitif", une commission d'experts remet ce mardi 10 novembre à Emmanuel Macron des propositions pour répondre aux risques soulevés par l'essor de l'intelligence artificielle générative, parmi lesquelles encadrer l'anthropomorphisme et la flagornerie, mieux protéger les mineurs et évaluer les modèles avant leur mise sur le marché.

Les risques de la délégation cognitive

Popularisée par des agents conversationnels comme ChatGPT d'OpenAI, Gemini de Google ou Claude d'Anthropic, l'IA générative est désormais utilisée par plus de la moitié des Français, plaçant la France au cinquième rang mondial des usages, selon ce rapport. Près de 70 % des 15-24 ans y ont recours régulièrement.

Cette commission de neuf experts, baptisée "IA générative et vulnérabilités", avait été chargée par le gouvernement d'examiner "les risques et les vulnérabilités engendrés par les usages grand public" de ces outils, notamment pour la santé mentale des plus jeunes.

Les conclusions de ce rapport, que l'AFP a pu consulter, interviennent après 55 auditions de professionnels de santé, de la recherche, d'entreprises ou encore d'associations de protection de l'enfance. Les experts soulèvent plusieurs risques liés à l'utilisation des IA génératives, notamment "d'ordre cognitif" avec la "délégation de fonctions cérébrales essentielles", comme la réflexion, la prise de décision ou l'esprit critique.

"Le premier enjeu est l'affaiblissement cognitif. C'est attractif, on y délègue des compétences. Puisqu'on y délègue des compétences, on ne les acquiert pas. C'est une problématique pour les jeunes, mais c'est une problématique pour tous", explique à l'AFP le professeur de psychiatrie Raphaël Gaillard, coprésident de cette commission.

Désinformation et dépendance à l'IA

Les experts insistent sur le risque lié à la désinformation: ces "dispositifs deviennent des sources d'informations dont on ne garantit pas la qualité", souligne le professeur, qui met en garde contre un risque "d'affaiblissement démocratique".

Ils mettent aussi en évidence le "risque de dépendance" émotionnelle lié notamment à "l'anthropomorphisation" des IA qui ont tendance à se présenter comme des interlocuteurs humains et à la "flagornerie", consistant à valider ou flatter l'utilisateur parfois au détriment de la vérité.

"On crée un registre de relations émotionnelles qui peut avoir vocation à se substituer à l'interaction" humaine, "c'est un système disponible en permanence, qui n'a pas d'autre intention que de vous garder en ligne", note M. Gaillard.

Mieux protéger la santé mentale et les mineurs

Parmi les 18 recommandations, la commission appelle ainsi à mieux encadrer ces mécanismes pour préserver "l'autonomie décisionnelle", la santé mentale des utilisateurs et la loyauté des interactions. Elle préconise de développer une politique nationale ambitieuse d'éducation à l'IA pour permettre à chacun d'en maitriser les usages et les risques, et renforcer l'esprit critique.

Parmi les mesures proposées figurent l'instauration d'évaluations indépendantes avant et après la mise sur le marché des systèmes d'IA générative, l'accès des autorités et chercheurs agréés aux données d'entraînement, d'usage et de monétisation des modèles, ainsi que la création d'un "protocole national de réponse aux crises informationnelles liées à l'IA".

Les experts, qui estiment que l'IA générative a accéléré certaines formes de violences numériques, notamment les deepfakes, appellent à "renforcer la répression de la création de contenus à caractère sexuel non consentis et pédocriminels" générés par IA.

La commission recommande aussi d'imposer un niveau élevé de protection pour les systèmes accessibles aux mineurs, avec le blocage des requêtes jugées dangereuses et un filtrage renforcé des contenus.

"Economie de la cognition"

Elle met aussi en garde contre l'émergence d'une "économie de la cognition": le modèle économique des IA génératives étant encore "en cours de consolidation" la commission appelle à "la plus grande vigilance" sur le risque d'exploitation des facultés cognitives, des émotions et des profils psychologiques des utilisateurs, notamment à travers des formes de publicités intégrées aux réponses des agents conversationnels.

Disant ne pas "vouloir mettre un boulet au pied de l'économie française ni européenne", les experts appellent Emmanuel Macron à "prendre des décisions".

"Si on ne prend pas ces décisions, les trois grands risques que nous avons évoqués", l'externalisation cognitive, la dépendance affective et les risques démocratiques liés à la désinformation, "on les subira", alerte M. Gaillard.

Emmanuel Macron a estimé lundi dans une interview au quotidien Les Echos qu'il fallait "interdire" l'intelligence artificielle là où elle présente un "risque" pour les enfants, leur "santé mentale, leur cerveau".

review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
Date: 2026-11-10T19:12:11+00:00
Source language: un
Original headline: Trust but Verify: Implementing Frontier AI Policy in California and Beyond
English normalization: Trust but Verify: Implementing Frontier AI Policy in California and Beyond
Collected full article body: What the New Democratic Congress Can (and Can’t) Do on Foreign Policy

Democrats now have the gavel and the purse, but the executive branch still pulls the levers on the U.S. role in the world.

- +10

James M. Acton, Dan Baer, Mark Baldassare, …

The choices California makes while implementing its frontier AI law has ramifications for AI governance in the United States and around the world.

In the year since California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act passed, also known as Senate Bill 53 (SB 53), artificial intelligence (AI) has made striking advances in areas ranging from mathematics to coding. At the same time, previous hypothetical risks posed by frontier AI systems have become serious, documented concerns. For example, models have found and exploited previously unknown software vulnerabilities and gained unauthorized access to external databases. As AI capabilities continue to improve, such incidents are likely to become more frequent and consequential.

Policymakers recognize the need to respond but face an evidence dilemma: AI evolves so quickly that responding prematurely risks entrenching ineffective policies, while delaying action could leave society vulnerable to serious risks. SB 53 aims to alleviate this dilemma by generating more evidence about AI risks to inform future policies. It trusts frontier AI companies, which hold much of the relevant technical expertise, to design and implement appropriate risk management practices and disclose the evidence behind them. In parallel, the approach empowers government bodies to verify industry claims about risks and the effectiveness of those practices. This “trust but verify” approach, first outlined in the California Report on Frontier AI Policy,1 combines flexibility with independent accountability.

This report aims to guide the implementation of “trust but verify” approaches such as SB 53 and maximize the chances they accomplish their goals. The design choices California makes at the beginning of implementation—such as which companies should be subject to these policies, how detailed frontier AI frameworks should be, and how to triage information about AI incidents—will ground how California manages risks for years to come.

These questions matter not just in California but also around the world as governments grapple with the challenge of how to govern advanced AI systems. SB 53 has already inspired similar frameworks in New York and Illinois. Even where “trust but verify” frameworks are not adopted in their entirety, many of the most important questions this report examines will remain relevant. For example, many governments will want to have confidence that models have undergone appropriate safety testing before they allow models to be deployed, or receive incident reports when models cause serious harm within their borders. As the federal government grapples with similar questions, California’s experiment in frontier AI governance and implementation can offer real-world evidence to support thoughtful federal policy.

SB 53 will not, and should not, be the final chapter in the story of how the United States governs advanced AI systems. California will need to strengthen its evaluation and assessment ecosystem, ensure that sufficient information on serious incidents is reported to the government, and respond to the novel challenges posed by potential recursive self-improvement—when AI fully automates AI R&D, potentially causing an intelligence explosion. However, it represents a critical first step that will inform the policies that follow. Given the profound uncertainty over the trajectory and pace of AI development, generating substantial evidence on AI’s capabilities and risks and developing a robust verification ecosystem can help policymakers make better decisions in the months and years to come.

Because this report bridges broad policy principles and technical implementation decisions, it is designed for multiple audiences. To serve them all, it is structured in three parts: Foregrounding, Foundations, and Frontiers.

Many readers will seek a general understanding of the “trust but verify” architecture. Part 1: Foregrounding explains the law’s underlying logic, previews SB 53’s statutory requirements, and draws broader lessons for implementing frontier AI policy.

Some readers will want to go one level deeper and understand the broad logic of each component of the “trust but verify” architecture. The introductions to each chapter in parts 2 and 3 explain why each component matters, how it is reflected in SB 53, and the key implementation trade-offs it raises. Readers can therefore grasp the core argument of each chapter from its introduction alone.

Finally, some readers will be deep in the trenches on difficult implementation decisions. For them, this report serves as a reference on key implementation challenges while acknowledging that in a fast-evolving field such as frontier AI policy, some questions will inevitably remain unresolved.

Scott R. Singer, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

Jon Bateman, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace

The first real test for any significant law arises not when it is enacted but when it is implemented. For frontier AI policy, that test is now underway in California.

In 2025, California—the epicenter of both global AI innovation and AI governance discussions—resolved one of the first chapters of the debate around how to govern the most advanced AI models with the passage of SB 53, the first frontier AI statute in the United States.2 Two states have followed closely, adopting many of the statute’s core provisions: In New York, the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act was signed in December 2025,3 while in Illinois the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315) was signed in July 2026.4

Policy design and implementation design are closely connected. Statutes shape the broad contours of policy direction. But whether policy works effectively depends on a series of small but consequential decisions made during implementation. Thoughtful implementation is thus essential to translating policy design into practice.

But implementation is notoriously difficult, and the speed and uncertain trajectory of frontier AI development introduces novel challenges in both statute and implementation design. This report seeks to explain the logic underlying the first wave of frontier AI policy, inform the implementation choices that will determine these laws’ effectiveness, and identify gaps that can inform the productive evolution of “trust but verify” policies as further evidence accumulates on capabilities, benefits, and risks.

California’s frontier AI policy rests on a simple premise: Equipping governments with better evidence of frontier AI’s emerging capabilities, benefits, and risks can strengthen public trust and support better-informed policymaking as the technology evolves. It seeks to navigate between two potential failure modes: Overly prescriptive policies could prematurely lock in ineffective arrangements, while waiting to build even the basic scaffolding for governance could leave society vulnerable to serious risks. Given deep uncertainty about the technology’s future trajectory and societal impacts, frontier AI policy needs to work effectively across a range of plausible futures and adapt as new evidence accumulates. Early frontier AI policy should therefore focus on creating mechanisms that generate and transmit evidence from companies to government and the public and strengthening the ecosystem to enable independent verification and accountability of frontier AI companies. This theory underlies this report’s intellectual ancestor, the California Report on Frontier AI Policy, commissioned by the governor of California.5

Since the California Report was published in 2025, the evidence base has materially changed. That report warned of “especially striking” improvements in frontier AI capabilities in biology, noted that frontier AI companies could not rule out that AI could “significantly assist with high impact cyber attacks,” and highlighted deceptive behavior and threats to human control as “concrete empirical evidence” of behaviors that “possibly foreshadow future harm.”6

Now, several of these concerns have become concrete.

These real-world episodes show that managing AI’s material risks is increasingly urgent. But the fact that AI progress is moving so quickly necessitates an approach that preserves flexibility.

“Trust but verify” approaches seek to strike this balance. Frontier AI companies have unique technical capacity to develop risk mitigation practices, which they document through frontier AI frameworks. The results of those efforts can then be subjected to multiple forms of independent scrutiny: Third-party evaluators can verify what developer assessments claim; incident reports can generate evidence about serious risks models pose; and whistleblower protections generate accountability by providing insiders with a channel to disclose when company practices do not match stated commitments. The purpose of this report is to explain how to design these components well so that they generate the evidence policymakers need and enable robust government accountability to support public trust in a technology that is deeply integrated into people’s daily lives.

To inform the implementation of “trust but verify” approaches, this report is broken into three main sections.

The first section, entitled “Foregrounding,” is the intellectual backbone for the rest of the report. It explains what SB 53 requires and how the statute has served as a template for other states. It also provides critical context, leveraging cross-disciplinary insight and full-spectrum evidence from AI development and governance, history, legal analysis, and modeling and simulation to inform cross-cutting themes in this report.

The second section is “Foundations.” “Trust but verify” is an interconnected system; deficiencies in any of its foundational components compromise the others. In particular, four implementation choices will shape whether SB 53’s mechanisms reinforce each other: how much detail frontier AI frameworks must offer to enable independent scrutiny, how incident reporting is designed to generate situational awareness, how whistleblower protections create usable channels for surfacing risk, and whether the ecosystem for independent assessment and evaluation develops the capacity and access it needs to conduct meaningful testing and oversight.

The third section, “Frontiers,” discusses emerging challenges for frontier AI governance. To begin with, the most advanced systems are only deployed internally for frontier AI companies’ own use, meaning they are the least visible to both governments and the public. So designing effective reports on internal deployments raises unresolved scoping and operational challenges. In addition, governments will need to update the thresholds to determine who is subject to what requirements over time as both the technology and its attendant risks evolve. And third, how state policy interacts with federal policy—and what aspects should be federalized—is one of the most consequential open questions in U.S. frontier AI governance.

Whether California policymakers can keep pace with the technology they seek to govern depends to a considerable extent on the implementation design choices made in the next six to twelve months. Real-world incidents are already testing California’s ability to respond to incidents, monitor and evaluate risks, and prevent AI systems from causing unacceptable levels of harm. Early design choices will create path dependencies for future policy efforts;10 the evidence generated now will inform the next generation of frontier AI laws in California and around the world.

Many of the mechanisms required by SB 53 would function better if implemented nationally, and many of the frontier AI governance ideas that have emerged from California enjoy bipartisan support in Congress. But absent federal action, California can engage in “purposeful placeholding”: creating expedient frontier AI policies that support the public interest absent federal action. This theory also applies to implementation. California can develop not just statutory requirements but also best practices in implementation that can support policymaking in Washington, DC, as well as globally.

Carnegie California links developments in California and the West Coast with national and global conversations around technology, democracy, and trans-Pacific relationships. At a distance from national capitals, and located in one of the world’s great experiments in pluralist democracy, Carnegie California engages a wide array of stakeholders as partners in its research and policy engagement.

SB 53 is both the first law in the United States governing frontier AI development and an early example of a broader “trust but verify” architecture that is already shaping how other states approach frontier AI governance. Understanding this model requires looking at the law’s substantive provisions, which institutions are responsible for implementing them, and how other jurisdictions have built on its core provisions.

This chapter provides that grounding. First, it explains the statutory requirements of SB 53. Second, it identifies the parts of California’s bureaucracy tasked with implementing those requirements. Third, it explains how SB 53 has served as a template for New York’s RAISE Act11 and Illinois’s SB 315,12 underscoring both the areas of emerging convergence in U.S. frontier AI policy and the ways that other states have built on or modified California’s approach.

Developer- and model-based thresholds: SB 53 is designed to cover the largest AI developers and the models most likely to pose catastrophic risks while avoiding regulatory burdens on smaller companies and less capable systems.13 The law defines a “large frontier developer” as a company with more than $500 million in gross revenues over the preceding calendar year. A “frontier model” is one trained using more than 10²6 floating point operations (FLOPS)—a metric that encompasses pretraining as well as subsequent fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. For most requirements, both thresholds need to be triggered, meaning that most of the law’s requirements apply only to the most compute-intensive models developed by the largest AI companies. Today, outside analysts estimate that only a few models exceed the compute threshold, including recent offerings from OpenAI and SpaceXAI, but other major labs will likely cross it soon.14

Although compute thresholds attempt to capture the most risky models, models that fall under the FLOPS threshold are not necessarily risk free. For example, DeepSeek’s latest models would not be captured by this threshold, even though testing by the U.S. Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) in 2025 indicates they are far more vulnerable to hijacking and jailbreaking than similar models from OpenAI and Anthropic.15 Furthermore, algorithmic breakthroughs and efficiency gains could mean that more capable—and risky—models are trained under 10²6 FLOPS. Recognizing this, the law requires the California Department of Technology (CDT) to write an annual report beginning in 2027 that would inform whether the thresholds for frontier models and large frontier developers should be updated.

Catastrophic risks: SB 53 focuses many of its provisions on the most serious potential risks caused by AI. It defines this “catastrophic risk” as the possibility that the development, storage, or use of a frontier model will materially contribute to either more than fifty deaths or serious injuries or more than $1 billion in economic damages resulting from AI-assisted creation or release of a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapon; cyber attacks or serious crimes caused by an AI system without meaningful human oversight; or AI activity that evades the control of the AI’s developer or user.

This focus on catastrophic risks comes amid growing evidence that both capabilities and risks have increased over the past year. At the same time, important challenges such as child safety and labor market impacts are not categorized as catastrophic and therefore fall outside SB 53’s scope.

Frontier AI frameworks: SB 53 requires major AI developers to publish safety frameworks that explain how the company will test its models for the risk of catastrophic harm, implement protections against those risks, respond to dangerous incidents, and secure its systems from unauthorized access. The law does not specify what standards or methods a company needs to put in its framework, but once it has laid them out, the law requires the company to follow them. If a company alters its framework, it must publish the updated framework—along with a justification for the change—within thirty days. Companies must review their frameworks at least annually and update them as appropriate. Frontier AI frameworks provide transparency into developers’ safety practices while also creating a baseline against which those practices can be assessed and enforced.

As well as publishing its risk frameworks, the company must periodically send an assessment of any catastrophic risks created by its internal use of its models, including if a frontier model circumvents oversight mechanisms, to the California Office of Emergency Services (OES).

Transparency reports: In addition to the overall framework, developers will have to publish information each time they release a new frontier model in California. How much they have to report depends on whether they cross the threshold for large frontier developers. All developers will have to publish basic information about new models, including intended uses, languages, modalities, and terms of service. Large developers must also explain how they complied with their frontier frameworks, including the results of any catastrophic risk assessments and the role played by third-party evaluators in testing the model. (They are allowed to redact information to protect trade secrets, their own cybersecurity, public safety, or U.S. national security.) These transparency reports are therefore designed to translate developers’ broader safety commitments into model-specific evidence.16

Incident reporting: The law requires frontier developers to report certain critical safety incidents to an appropriate authority. There is a high bar for what needs to be reported: only incidents causing death, bodily injury, or materialized catastrophic harm, plus deceptive model behavior that materially increases catastrophic risk. That is a significantly higher standard than in earlier drafts of SB 53. The company compliance burden will be lower, but less information sharing might also hamper the ability of governments to address future harms.

Developers have fifteen days to file a report, unless the incident poses imminent risk of death or serious bodily injury, in which case they must notify an appropriate authority within twenty-four hours.

Whistleblower protections: SB 53 strengthens whistleblower protections for specific “covered employees” responsible for assessing, managing, or addressing risk of critical safety incidents. The law requires large frontier developers to create anonymous whistleblowing channels. Covered employees are protected from retaliation for using those channels or for reporting information to the federal or state governments, if they had reasonable cause to believe that their employer’s activities posed a substantial danger to public health or safety resulting from a catastrophic risk. These protections strengthen accountability by giving insiders a protected channel to report when developers’ actual safety practices diverge from their stated commitments.

Internal deployments: The framework must also cover internal deployments, as SB 53 recognizes that risks can emerge from models that are used only by company employees, not the general public. Before deploying a frontier model publicly or using it extensively within the company, the framework must explain what risk assessments and mitigations the company has in place and why it believes they are adequate. As part of the assessment of internal deployments, the law requires companies to address the risk that their models may circumvent internal oversight mechanisms—a provision that reflects growing concerns about advanced AI systems evading the safety controls meant to govern them. By covering internal deployments, the law extends oversight to systems that are not publicly released but that still generate important information about emerging capabilities and risks.

Federal deference: SB 53 builds in a novel mechanism for federal deference: If developers are already reporting incidents under federal laws, regulations, or guidance documents with similar standards, OES can declare those standards equivalent to SB 53’s reporting requirements and allow companies to fulfill California’s rules by meeting the federal rule. This provision should allow California’s framework to avoid redundant compliance burdens if new federal requirements emerge while preserving its ability to protect its citizens.

No external auditing: An earlier version of the bill would have required third-party audits for some AI systems. This provision was removed before final passage. An auditing requirement was passed, however, in Illinois’s SB 315.17

Enforcement: SB 53’s enforcement centers on civil penalties and oversight by the California attorney general. Large frontier developers that fail to meet their reporting obligations, or that make false or misleading statements, can face fines of up to $1 million per violation if the California attorney general brings civil action. These penalties thus provide accountability for the law’s disclosure requirements.

Implementation of SB 53 is distributed across three existing bodies in California’s government (rather than concentrated in a dedicated frontier AI policy office): the Office of Emergency Services (OES), California Department of Technology (CDT), and the Office of the Attorney General (AG). As such, California’s AI policy implementation leverages cross-domain expertise in emergency response, legal enforcement, and technology policy.

OES carries the heaviest operational load. It is tasked with creating mechanisms to receive developer reports on how they assess catastrophic risks, including assessment for internal deployments. Furthermore, OES is in charge of reviewing critical safety incidents and creating an annual, summarized report to be transmitted to the legislature, the governor, the federal government, or appropriate state agencies. Finally, OES is empowered to carry out SB 53’s novel mechanism of federal deference for incident reporting.

CDT’s role is primarily advisory and informs adjustments to scoping. It reviews whether definitions for “frontier model,” “frontier developer,” and “large frontier developer” remain fit for purpose and submits recommendations to the legislature.

Finally, AG holds the enforcement function. It serves as the state channel for whistleblower disclosures and can impose civil penalties on frontier AI developers that fail to meet these requirements: failing to transmit or publish reports or documents, failing to report a required incident, or failing to follow their frontier AI framework.

In addition to SB 53, California has taken several other steps to create a governance framework for frontier AI (see table 1). In particular, it has begun laying the groundwork for an ecosystem of third-party audits. In September 2026, Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 813 and AB 1405, which set out initial, high-level rules for the operation of independent verification organizations (IVOs) and AI auditing groups in California. SB 813 requires the California government to develop, by January 1, 2028, a process to designate third-party organizations as IVOs that can assess AI developers’ and deployers’ compliance with state law.18 Under SB 813, the Government Operations Agency (GovOps) will set out criteria for IVO designation, including the metrics and methods for assessing AI risks, technical expertise of IVO staff, and independence from the AI industry.

AB 1405, meanwhile, requires third-party AI auditing organizations to register with the California government beginning January 1, 2029, if they are to carry out audits of AI systems for compliance with state law.19 Registered AI auditors will have to report information about their operations and auditing standards to GovOps and comply with state-set standards for independence and objectivity. Together, the two laws may help spur the development of a third-party auditing ecosystem and allow California to begin developing standards for the process and substance of those audits.

The rapid diffusion of SB 53’s core provisions suggests that a common “trust but verify” model is beginning to emerge across states (see table 2). Both the RAISE Act, signed into New York state law in December 2025,20 and SB 315, signed into Illinois state law in July 2026,21 build on SB 53. The states have converged around frontier AI frameworks, incident reporting, and oversight of internal deployments, while developing different approaches to administrative structure, reporting timelines, whistleblower protections, and independent auditing.

The RAISE Act deploys many of SB 53’s definitions, such as those for “catastrophic risk,” “critical safety incident,” and “foundation model,” as well as its thresholds.22 It also incorporates several of SB 53’s central requirements, including frontier AI frameworks, incident reporting, and oversight of internal deployments. However, RAISE differs from SB 53 in meaningful ways. First, whereas SB 53’s implementation is divided across a number of bodies, RAISE created a new AI governance–focused office, the Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust (DIGIT), housed within the New York State Department of Financial Services. That office is also empowered to create new transparency requirements through regulation. In contrast to SB 53, RAISE does not provide added statutory whistleblower protections; New York’s background whistleblower protections may already apply in cases where SB 53 added coverage in California. Finally, whereas SB 53 requires critical safety incidents to be reported within fifteen days, the RAISE Act reduces that window to seventy-two hours.

Illinois’s SB 315 is the third law modeled on SB 53. It incorporates all the same core components with one important addition: It requires annual third-party audits for large frontier developers. The auditor writes a report explaining whether the developer has complied with its frontier AI framework as well as outlining any areas where it might have deviated. These audits can verify compliance with a developer’s stated framework, but they do not necessarily ensure that the framework itself is high quality. SB 315 also departs from both California and New York in its administering body: Reporting mechanisms, guidance, and annual reports are the responsibility of the Illinois Emergency Management Agency and Office of Homeland Security, acting in consultation with the state attorney general. And unlike RAISE, but like SB 53, SB 315 creates dedicated whistleblower protections and internal reporting processes for covered employees.23

These differences not only reflect state-level variation in risk management needs—for example, differences in baseline whistleblower protections—but also provide opportunities for California to learn from other states’ policy experiments. For example, California should closely track whether consolidating frontier AI risk management responsibilities, as New York and Illinois have done, improves efficiency and makes better use of limited technical expertise. Learning from other jurisdictions’ successes and failures can help California refine its frontier AI policy approach.

Taken together, these laws suggest a growing convergence around the core components of “trust but verify,” even as states continue to iterate on both their substantive requirements and the ways that those requirements are administered and enforced.

The observed social impacts of a rapidly changing technology are a necessary but incomplete foundation for developing sound governance policies. Unlike domains such as pharmaceuticals and medical devices, which can rely on evidence generated from clinical trials to ensure safety, AI lacks an analogous evidence-generation model. Absent one, AI policies may rapidly become outdated and fail to respond to present risks. Indeed, history also reminds us of failure modes from previous technologies. In the tobacco industry, companies intentionally undermined independent research that would have provided consumers with rigorous evidence of the products’ effects on their health; in the case of fossil fuels, rigorous modeling of future harms sat within industry without a mechanism to promote public transparency.24 These lessons, discussed extensively in the California Report, underscore the uniquely important role that governments can play in strengthening the evidence base and enabling independent accountability.

Building on that foundation, this chapter highlights three key themes: 1) how implementation decisions shape policy impact, 2) the centrality of talent to deliver effective implementation, and 3) the importance of credible mechanisms to ensure enforcement incentives operate as intended.

Implementation is hard. Many of the most promising ideas at the stage of policy passage fail because they are implemented poorly or never at all. In its short history, AI policy has far too often suffered a similar fate. A December 2022 paper from the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) revealed that of three pillars of U.S. AI strategy developed from 2019 to 2020, fewer than 40 percent of the forty-five legal requirements had been implemented.25 Across historical experiences in domains ranging from public health to transportation safety, the distance between promise and outcomes is a function of the approach to implementation.

The field of public policy has long acknowledged the novel challenges that can emerge at the implementation stage. Policies designed well in the abstract, once they reach the implementation stage, may face unanticipated technical challenges, challenges navigating bureaucracies and coordinating across different departments, and sophisticated chains of action where challenges implementing one part can negatively impact the other elements of implementation. Here, the canonical text Implementation, a 1979 book by Jeffrey L. Pressman and Aaron Wildavsky that offers a rigorous analysis of a California project that failed to live up to its potential promise, offers useful lessons.26

The first is that implementation design decisions are natural extensions of a theory of how policy architectures achieve socially desirable outcomes. As Pressman and Wildavsky write in Implementation, “Policies imply theories.”27 In the case of the Economic Development Administration’s Oakland project, which was the subject matter of Implementation, the hypothesis of the administration’s work was: “If the federal government, through the Economic Development Administration, provides $23 million in loans and grants to enterprises in Oakland, and if these enterprises agree to hire minorities after spending the money, then facilities will be built leading to the creation of new jobs that will go to minorities.”28 Yet this hypothesis turned on several sub-mechanisms and assumptions that could stall the causal chain. They included poorly designed incentives for companies to hire long-term unemployed workers as opposed to temporary contractors, the need to build additional monitoring and sanction mechanisms to verify whether companies complied, and gaps between what was measured empirically—the percentage of minority workers hired—and the underlying goal of structural change.29

For “trust but verify” architectures, the hypothesis is directly tied to solving the problem posed by the evidence dilemma: the fact that these statutory mechanisms will only work as intended if their implementation actively and constructively supports evidence generation. The architecture supposes that policies will incentivize greater evidence generation, generated evidence will flow to key government stakeholders and the public, and thoughtfully dispersing this information more broadly can inform next steps in AI policy. But embedded in that causal chain are several decisions that will require sign-off by many stakeholders; seemingly small failures at the implementation layer can collectively undermine the hypothesis underlying policy design. If poor decisions are made at any of these key junctures, the evidence environment on frontier AI capabilities and risks could suffer from the same information asymmetries that doomed the public interest in the cases of tobacco and fossil fuels.30

The project appeared unusually well positioned for success: It had a major, well-resourced recipient in the Port of Oakland, substantial federal funding, and a relatively straightforward set of development projects.31 But when it came time to implement the policies, each step had to consider a wide range of stakeholders, requiring many negotiations and interdependencies that compounded exponentially over time.32 Each “clearance”—each instance in which an agreement had to be reached for implementation to continue—was a separate hurdle.33 For path dependencies in implementation, even if every actor at every stage were 90 percent likely to agree promptly, the odds of cumulative success fall below a coin flip after just seven decision points.34 Of course, this stylized mathematical model overstates the independence of each decision. But it nonetheless offers a useful insight: Even well-intentioned actors with meaningfully varying incentives may struggle to reach consensus, and the impact of these delays may compound over time.

The compounding nature of challenges and delays to implementation creates a tremendous burden for policymakers at the implementation stage; as this report highlights, implementing “trust but verify” frameworks will create a substantial number of small decisions that in aggregate will determine the statute’s effectiveness. By outlining these potential junctures and trade-offs ahead of time, policymakers may be better equipped to develop an approach that integrates competing perspectives together.
