Legal effect. The federal standard need not have the force of law. Guidance documents issued by federal agencies do not necessarily have binding legal effect. Typically, agency regulations that create civil or criminal penalties must be issued through specific regulatory processes.366 Nonbinding standards or legal interpretations usually do not have to follow those procedures. SB 53 suggests that such nonbinding documents can serve as federal substitutes for California law by making any company that agrees to follow them liable under state law for violating the federal standard. In considering such nonbinding guidance, OES should consider how it will judge compliance with an otherwise nonbinding document, including its ability to collect the necessary information and the interpretation that state and federal courts might give to the provisions of the federal standard.

Assessing equivalence. SB 53 does not specify in what respects the federal standard must be substantially equivalent to or stricter than California’s requirements, or whether equivalence should be judged by outcomes (whether the law achieves the same effect) or process (whether it follows the same steps). Because the precise effect of any such law may be difficult to assess ex ante, California may wish to ensure that, at a minimum, three central elements are a close match between the state and federal laws: (1) the definition of a reportable incident, (2) the details a developer must include in its report, and (3) the deadline. Each of these goes to the core purpose of the law: the ability of the government to respond to and mitigate catastrophic risks from AI. A federal rule that covers a narrower scope of incidents, requires companies to omit information California requires, or has significantly looser deadlines may not achieve the same benefits as SB 53.

In the case where a federal rule imposes stricter requirements, the considerations are different. There would no longer be a risk of the law failing to capture activity that California intended to cover. Instead, an important consideration for OES would be whether the federal rule has independent legal effect. If it does not, then by incorporating it into state law, California might be imposing an additional compliance burden on developers beyond the requirements of SB 53. Depending on the nature of the federal rule, that burden might upset the balance created by SB 53. California will have to consider whether the benefit of adopting a single standard outweighs those costs. If, on the other hand, the federal rule has the force of law, then designation by OES will remove a compliance burden by avoiding double reporting.

Information sharing. SB 53 regulates how information from incident reports is shared within and outside the California government. The law requires OES to create annual reports summarizing certain information from incident reports and allows it to transmit incident reports to the California legislature and other government offices. OES may wish to consider whether any federal standard should have similar public and internal reporting provisions. On the one hand, requiring such provisions may foster public transparency and internal government cooperation, while on the other hand, OES may conclude that the federal government is best placed to determine how and whether information from such reports should be communicated within and between the branches. Here, OES may wish to rely on a holistic assessment of the effectiveness of information sharing provisions rather than on the need for a specific match with SB 53.

Beyond the mandatory criteria required by SB 53, OES may wish to consider additional factors in determining whether to designate a federal rule. Because California law makes the choice to designate discretionary, OES can take such factors into account.367

To inform the selection of such criteria, California may wish to consider the experience of the federal government in evaluating state programs as substitutes for federal regulatory schemes. One of the most developed is the rubric used by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration to review state workplace safety programs.368 In addition to several mandatory criteria, that body also considers such factors as the resources of the relevant agency, the state’s enforcement track record, the state’s ability to update its rules to maintain their effectiveness, and the extent of any waivers the state issues.369 With SB 53, the direction reverses: It would be California assessing a federal agency under such factors.

Factors California may wish to consider include:

Ability to judge compliance. Because SB 53 makes the failure to follow a designated federal standard a violation of California law, OES will need a way to determine when a violation has occurred. This may be most straightforward if the federal standard comes from a statute or regulation with the force of law. In that case, OES may be able to rely on federal authorities to monitor compliance, with the California government able to determine after the fact whether it should independently investigate any alleged noncompliance reported or prosecuted by the federal government. If, on the other hand, the standard is nonbinding, OES will need to rely on public or nonpublic information shared by the relevant federal agency to determine in the first instance whether it believes a violation has occurred.

To that end, OES may also wish to consider the extent to which the federal agency has agreed to publish information relating to incident reporting and to share nonpublic information with OES. Such nonpublic information would need to be extensive enough to give OES the ability to judge compliance. The California government may also retain the ability to independently investigate adherence to a designated federal standard, but such investigations may well prove more productive if federal information sharing is agreed upon in advance. Similarly, OES may wish to seek an agreement with the relevant federal agency that it will cooperate, in compliance with relevant federal law, in OES investigations.

Durability. Designation of a federal standard will bring the best protection for the public and the largest benefits for developers when companies can rely on a stable federal regime. OES may thus wish to consider the likely durability of any federal rule. Federal standards sit on a spectrum. Guidance documents can be withdrawn, modified, or replaced without notice, which may leave companies unsure of their obligations under California law or force OES to assess on short notice whether each new iteration still meets its requirements. Regulations promulgated through notice and comment rulemaking are more durable, as agencies must typically go through the same process to modify them.370 Statutes are the most durable of all, although the precise durability will depend on how much discretion the law leaves the relevant agency.

A less stable standard need not be disqualifying. A nonbinding federal document may adequately address the risks covered by SB 53. In such circumstances, OES may wish to specify that California law will incorporate a specific version of the guidance, and any changes will not be reflected in California law until OES has reviewed them, or that a change to, or withdrawal of, the guidance will cause SB 53’s reporting obligations to snap back into place.

Expertise, authority, and resources of the federal agency. Where California is satisfied that a federal standard meets SB 53’s objectives, it may still wish to consider the federal government’s practical ability to collect, understand, and act on incident reports—and its ability to enforce the law. Relevant indicators might include the funding, staffing, expertise, and enforcement authority of the federal agency in question. California should have confidence that the agency will be able to monitor compliance, update its rules as the technology evolves, and effectively investigate potential violations.

Process. Some of these factors may be difficult to assess up front or may change over time. An agency’s budget, staffing, and technical depth can vary from administration to administration. A standard that met the needs of the technology at one moment may grow stale if it is not updated. Because SB 53 requires OES to revoke a designation if the relevant criteria are no longer met, it may wish to establish the procedures through which it will ensure the continued effectiveness of the federal standard. This might involve a regular review process, public notice of California’s reconsideration, and the opportunity for the public to submit data and reviews to OES.371 Establishing such a process in advance may also have the benefit of avoiding any perception that California is singling out a particular federal standard for political reasons.

Incident reporting is only one slice of SB 53. California officials implementing SB 53 may nonetheless take account of developments in other jurisdictions by crafting guidance and implementing requirements in a manner designed to harmonize relevant standards to the greatest extent permitted by the law, without diluting its goals.

More generally, if the broader “trust but verify” approach to AI governance succeeds at the state level, there will be a strong case for federalizing it. Each of the relevant factors counsels in favor of a federal approach. A single set of rules requiring developers to create and adhere to frontier AI safety frameworks would minimize the compliance burden on industry without sacrificing safety. Consumers and citizens have little need for such rules to be tailored to local preferences, as identical foundation models are served by a small handful of companies nationwide. At the same time, federalizing safety and reporting requirements would strengthen the work of federal evaluation bodies, especially CAISSI.

Federal expertise will also be essential. States, including California, are working to bring technical experts into government to oversee AI governance, but, as is outlined earlier in this report, the talent necessary to understand frontier AI capabilities, inform policy, and design mitigations is in short supply. Duplicating this effort across many different states will be far less efficient than creating centralized sources of expertise at the federal level.

Although unifying the “trust but verify” approach at the federal level would bring gains in efficiency, when it comes to some elements, such as whistleblower protections, the case for federal leadership is less apparent. Whistleblowing channels exist at both the state and federal levels, after all, and collecting such reports may not require the same level of expertise as frontier model evaluation. If states create successful systems, disrupting them may be costly.

SB 53 is a state law, but the questions it raises are national and even global. California acted because it has a responsibility to its citizens, and because the federal government has not yet set rules for the frontier developers whose models will shape the economy, public safety, and national security in the years ahead.

But acting first is not the same as acting alone. SB 53’s designation provision reflects the reality that the federal-state division of labor over AI will change as the federal government develops its approach. Such provisions can help smooth the handoff between state and federal governance. Many aspects of frontier AI are likely well suited to federal intervention, thanks to the national nature of the market for foundation models, the national security implications of transformative AI, and the need for regulatory expertise. The designation mechanism thus creates a standing offer: Once the federal government can adopt an effective incident reporting standard of its own, California is positioned to step back.

That approach is a model other states can use. New York and Illinois have both adopted frontier AI governance laws—the RAISE Act and SB 315—that parallel many aspects of SB 53, and SB 315 goes further by establishing interoperability with certain other regulatory regimes. If more states follow suit, analogous designation provisions may give any eventual federal standard a clear path to creating a uniform national rule. By precommitting to the conditions under which they will defer to federal authority, states can both reduce the risk of conflicting rules and demonstrate to federal policymakers what a workable, credible standard looks like. SB 53 will not be the last word in the federal-state conversation over frontier AI governance; it is an early move in a longer process.

The technologies that emerge from California will reshape how communities and societies operate around the United States and the world. Frontier AI is no exception. Governance ideas that have emerged in California will shape how companies with truly global reach operate; entities from all over the world have become part of a dynamic ecosystem that enables compliance with California’s law.

Whether SB 53 creates its designed impact will depend on a series of implementation choices now in front of California policymakers. The standards California sets for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, and the disclosure of internal deployments will determine whether “trust but verify” frameworks generate meaningful evidence and transparency. Decisions around incident reporting—what counts as a reportable incident, what information must be reported, and what the state does with reports once they arrive—will shape whether the state enables meaningful situational awareness. The whistleblower channels being built now will determine whether SB 53’s transparency measures will actually create accountability. Ultimately, these early implementation design choices will create path dependencies that shape future AI laws. Getting these decisions right—in California and in every jurisdiction that follows its lead—is of the utmost importance.

SB 53 is global in nature because its subject, frontier AI development, is global, and because the verification ecosystem it relies on—UK AISI, U.S. CAISSI, and independent third-party evaluators distributed across institutions—is necessarily transnational. Many of the law’s foundational components, such as frontier AI frameworks and scoping coverage, are explicitly grounded in both national and international standards, and ideas about these standards are being developed through global conversations. When companies demonstrate how they comply with frontier AI frameworks through transparency reports, they often do so by voluntarily submitting their models for testing not just to U.S. CAISSI but also to UK AISI. Other countries around the world—such as Australia, Canada, China, France, India, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea—have followed these examples and are building institutional capacity inside or closely connected to the government to understand and manage different AI risks. When one jurisdiction has a powerful idea in AI governance, others follow. The close mirroring of the RAISE Act and SB 315 to SB 53 highlights a pathway toward national harmonization and even global consensus: replicating the core parts of the paradigm while leaving sufficient space to tailor to local constituent needs.

California offers a domestic foundation for what will inevitably need to be a global effort to manage AI’s risks. “Trust but verify” only works fully when frontier developers’ employees, wherever they sit, have credible channels to surface evidence of catastrophic risk. California cannot create those channels outside its borders, but the protections it establishes inside them as well as the requirements it puts on companies doing business within the state set a template that other jurisdictions can adopt. The same logic applies to the rest of the paradigm: So long as they have no system to receive critical incident reports occurring within their borders, governments will lack both situational awareness and the ability to share an appropriate amount of information across borders. International AI risk management will bring unique security and legal challenges, but it begins with each country developing its own domestic, interoperable risk management infrastructures.

The model- and developer-level interventions SB 53 creates make the world safer. However, they are one part of a broader effort for global AI security. Misuse, malicious adaptation, and the harms that emerge only at the point of application sit downstream of those interventions and will require complementary measures by the jurisdictions where deployment occurs. Other jurisdictions will need to be part of a global, interconnected risk management effort that weaves model-level interventions with those downstream of AI developers. Well-developed “trust but verify” policies offer a foundation upon which these other efforts can build.

Every government has a stake in how California governs frontier AI because the technologies emerging from California will touch their citizens. The path toward the best outcomes is narrow, and the stakes are high. The choices California makes today will shape the future of frontier AI governance for decades to come.

review_queue.title: Identifying sleeper agents concealed within AI model neurons
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Microsoft
Date: 2026-11-10T23:00:00+00:00
Source language: un
Original headline: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
English normalization: Identifying sleeper agents concealed within AI model neurons
Collected full article body: Microsoft Research has released new threat research detailing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons to inject a short payload. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker’s command. And because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party models and internally developed models.

Key findings from Microsoft Research include:

- Software abuse and manipulation are familiar threats. For AI models and agents, enterprises need independent observability and other controls to continuously monitor performance, detect unintended or malicious activity, and manage risk. Satya Nadella recently outlined this approach in a blog post.

- A backdoored model can pass evaluations. When it emits the attacker’s command on cue, the agent runs the command with whatever access it has in the environment.

- The attack needs inference-only compute. If a machine has enough RAM to run a model, it has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it.

- Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously.

Microsoft has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. However, this research aligns with similar recent research by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively, highlighting the need to audit open weights like code.

Notably, Microsoft Research has also found that this threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. Using frontier agents as auditors can help automate the defense against this threat. More broadly, Microsoft Research’s approach demonstrates an adaptable process for securing AI agents: agents surface new security problems, and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

Learn more from the Microsoft Research Blog:

Mitigation and protection guidance

Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to defend against this threat as part of a broader defense-in-depth approach. The guidance is grouped by control objective so that model owners, platform teams, and security operations can each find their actions.

Audit model weights before deployment and after every update

- Diff every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. Legitimate fine-tunes and quantized versions change weights broadly and diffusely, while implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount. Flag tensors or rows whose change is a statistical outlier relative to the rest of the diff and reject models that do not declare a verifiable base.

- Use frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline. Microsoft Research found they are highly effective at finding anomalous structure in weights that manual inspection misses, which makes this step automatable at scale.

- Complement weight diffing with behavioral backdoor scanning of open-weight models, as described in Microsoft’s research on detecting backdoored language models at scale.

- Record audit results alongside the model in the registry, and state clearly to internal consumers that passing an audit reduces risk but does not guarantee safe behavior.

Secure model hubs and publishers

- Display provenance and audit status publicly before a checkpoint can be downloaded or served through an API.

- Scan every upload for anomalous neurons, weight patterns or behaviors, and state clearly that third-party checkpoints can be unsafe and that passing an audit does not guarantee safe behavior.

Treat every third-party model as untrusted until audited

- Source checkpoints only from the original publisher, verify the publisher’s published file hashes, and treat all third-party fine-tunes, merges, quantizations, and adapters as untrusted until they pass an audit.

- Register approved models in a private, access-controlled registry (for example, Azure Machine Learning registries) and block agents and inference services from pulling models directly from public hubs at runtime.

- Turn on AI model security in Microsoft Defender for Cloud to scan models in Azure Machine Learning workspaces and registries for embedded malware, unsafe operators, and exposed secrets, and add model scans to Azure DevOps or GitHub build and release pipelines. Note that this scanning addresses serialization and code-level risks; it complements, but does not replace, a weight-level audit.

- Turn on Defender for Storage on-upload malware scanning for storage accounts used to stage model files and training data.

Red team for hidden triggers

- Add trigger-hunting and backdoor scenarios to your AI red team plan. Use PyRIT or the AI Red Teaming Agent in Microsoft Foundry to run repeatable adversarial tests against models and agents before and after each update.

Contain what an agent can do if its model is compromised

- Run agents with least privilege. Give each agent its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID, scope its permissions to the minimum set of resources it needs, and use Conditional Access for agents to lblock unapproved or high-risk agent identities.

- Execute agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, such as Azure Container Apps dynamic sessions, and never expose host-side file write or shell tools to the model.

- Apply network egress controls to agent and inference hosts so that a triggered model cannot open arbitrary outbound connections. Allow only the endpoints the agent requires and turn on network protection in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.

- Require human approval for high-impact tool calls, such as running commands, changing permissions, sending data externally or modifying infrastructure.

- Apply attack surface reduction rules to devices that host local agents and inference servers, starting in audit mode.

Detect and block malicious agent behavior at runtime

- Turn on Microsoft Defender security for AI agents and configure real-time protection rules so Defender can audit and block risky tool invocations, secret exfiltration, and evasion techniques for Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio and Agent 365 agents, and runtime protection for local agents through Defender for Endpoint.

- Turn on threat protection for AI services in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, including suspicious prompt evidence, so the security operations center (SOC) receives alerts for jailbreak attempts, credential leakage in model responses and malicious URLs in AI interactions.

- Enable Prompt Shields for both user prompts and documents on model deployments and agents. Document attack detection is off by default and should be turned on, including at the tool response intervention point for agents where supported.

- Onboard every device and server that runs agents or local inference to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint in active mode so that suspicious child processes, persistence and outbound connections from agent host processes are detected.

Maintain inventory and governance of models and agents

- Use the AI agent inventory in the Microsoft Defender portal to discover agents, their tools, identities, and risk indicators.

- Use AI security posture management in Defender for Cloud to build an AI bill of materials (AI BOM) across Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Google Cloud Platform (GCP), so you know which models are deployed where.

- Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps and Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI to discover, sanction or block generative AI apps, and to monitor sensitive data in AI interactions.

- Map controls to the Microsoft catalog of AI defense capabilities, which groups supply-chain provenance, model hardening, runtime isolation and monitoring into a single framework aligned to MITRE ATLAS and the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications.

Learn more

For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog.

To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn, X (formerly Twitter), and Bluesky.

To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast.

review_queue.title: What Can Artificial Intelligence Do for Writers? (updated)
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Daily Nous
Date: 2026-11-11T14:21:54+00:00
Source language: un
Original headline: What May Artificial Intelligence Do for Writers? (updated)
English normalization: What Can Artificial Intelligence Do for Writers? (updated)
Collected full article body: When it comes to permissible uses of AI in professional writing, one philosopher argues that “anything that is acceptable to ask a human to do is, other things equal, acceptable for an LLM to do. (Equivalently, anything it would be wrong to ask a human to do is wrong to ask an LLM to do.)”

This “simple principle” was put forward by Kyle van Oosterum (Southampton) at his newsletter, Unchambered, several months ago.

The principle rules out, van Oosterum says, having an LLM write an article for you and you failing to acknowledge that. Writers are generally not morally permitted to “take credit for someone else’s work,” and that goes not just when the someone else is a someone but also when it is a something . But the principle doesn’t prohibit, he says, using an AI to “transcribe interviews, generate pushback on my… thesis, suggest trims when I’m over my word count, sharpen podcast interview questions, and perform a final fact check on columns and editorials.”

van Oosterum says:

The Simple Principle would, therefore, permit [a writer] to use an LLM to complete the very same tasks which are ‘ancillary’ to the main job. This point is crucial. The principle is compatible with the obviously-true idea that an author retains ultimate responsibility; just as one cannot blame a human assistant for a published error, the author remains the agent responsible for the final output.

Is van Oosterum’s principle a good one? The idea is to piggyback on the existing norms we have regarding authorship and assistance.

Keep in mind it was offered in something like blog post. Presumably, he would sharpen it up some were it to appear in a less casual venue. We can do a little of that work. Here is the original version again:

1. Anything that is acceptable to ask a human to do is, other things equal, acceptable for an LLM to do. (Equivalently, anything it would be wrong to ask a human to do is wrong to ask an LLM to do.)

To start, the language of “asking” is a distraction; the principle is supposed to be about the ethics of having AIs and other people complete tasks for you, not the ethics of asking them to do so. (Which is not to say that there might not be interesting ethical questions about asking.)

Now let’s turn to the ceteris paribus clause. I’m not quite sure what “other things equal” is supposed to refer to in the context of this principle. It can’t mean “provided no other possibly morally relevant issues besides the bare assigning of the task to a human or an LLM arise,” for what we’re interested in, when assessing the principle, is whether there are other morally relevant issues that tend to arise with this choice that it doesn’t adequately address. So I’m tempted to leave it out, and simply say that whatever results from our further refinement may be a defeasible principle.

Next, note that the parenthetical van Oosterum added to the principle (Equivalently…”) implies he meant it as a biconditional. Put in a form that makes that clear, and taking into account the other revisions, we get the following principle:

2. For professional writing, it is morally permissible to have an AI/LLM perform a writing-related task if and only if it is permissible to have a human perform that task.

What do you think?

A few preliminaries:

- The principle is being offered up for our consideration. That it may conflict with the extant policies of journals and other publications is beside the point.

- Humans and AIs have different capacities; each may be able to do things (or do things in certain ways, or for certain durations) that the other cannot. Does that matter for this principle? No. The principle is about permitted acts, not required ones. While ‘ought’ implies ‘can,’ ‘may’ does not.

- The principle is presumably intended for AIs/LLMs roughly as they are now. If their capacities significantly change, so too may the principle(s) that apply to it.

- That an act is morally permissible is not necessarily the only morally relevant thing to say about it.

Is this a good way to approach the ethics of authorship in the era of AI? Discussion welcome.

UPDATE: A reader draws my attention to a substantively similar principle put forward by Mark Robert Taylor (Calvin University) in an article published in January in the Journal of Philosophy of Education. In “The Obligation to Restrict AI in Student Writing” (PhilPapers link) Taylor says:

I am arguing against only those uses of AI which, were they performed by a person, such as a student’s classmate, would violate the academic values which forbid plagiarism. If a student is permitted to talk over essay ideas with a classmate, she ought to be permitted to discuss the same with AI. On the other hand, if a student is not permitted to submit an outline which her classmate wrote, she should not be permitted to submit an outline which was AI generated. If a student consults with an AI for ideas or actual phrasing, as she would a secondary source, this may be appropriate but only if the AI is properly cited in the way a secondary source must be. In other words, teachers ought, pragmatically, to treat student use of AI as they would student dependence on other people. My central contention is that teachers who allow students to use AI in cases where they would forbid dependence on other persons are in a position morally parallel to allowing plagiarism.

Taylor also discusses the article in a post at New Work in Philosophy.

review_queue.title: Robin Li first introduced the “Three Principles of Organizational Evolution”, predicting the next stage of AI to be intelligent organizations.
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: 新华网
Date: 2026-11-12T07:04:01+00:00
Source language: zh
Original headline: 李彦宏首提“组织进化三原则”，判断AI下一幕是智能组织
English normalization: Robin Li first introduced the “Three Principles of Organizational Evolution”, predicting the next stage of AI to be intelligent organizations.
Collected full article body: 11月12日，百度世界2026在北京举办。百度创始人李彦宏在开幕式上判断，人工智能的下一幕是“智能组织”，并首次提出“组织进化三原则”：打破岗位边界、沉淀隐性知识、设计流程闭环。“如果说，人工智能是新电能。那么，智能组织就是AI时代的新厂房，是生产力真正发生的地方。”

在李彦宏看来，如果AI技术的上游是能源，下游就是组织能力，“是一个不同于现在通行的科层制的AI原生组织体系，我们把它叫做智能组织。”

他类比工业时代的发展进程指出，AI没有产生预期的经济效益，是因为只更换了电机，没有重新设计工厂。“换一台AI新电机，只是起点；重新设计新厂房，才是分水岭。而这座新厂房，就是智能组织！”

本届大会期间，百度围绕“芯云模体”四层架构，发布多项成果：正式推出大模型交易平台词元所，发布文心大模型5.5 Flash预览版及两款文心应用模型；百度搭子、库库、百度一镜、伐谋四大智能体迎来升级；百度智能云正式发布天池1024卡超节点，昆仑芯公布新的产品计划，萝卜快跑全球化运营再提速。

组织进化有三原则，未来岗位将收敛为两类

大会开幕式上，李彦宏提出“组织进化三原则”。首先是打破岗位边界。在他看来，岗位是工业时代的单元，任务则是智能时代的单元，未来的组织就是一个任务的网络。“岗位不会消失，但会收敛，未来大致会分为两类岗位：一类是Builder，负责创造新东西；另一类是Seller，负责人与人之间的沟通和连接，让对方对你产生情感、建立信任。”

其次是沉淀隐性知识。企业的做事经验若只存在员工脑子里，就只是个体能力；只有显性化并沉淀到公司平台上，才构成组织智能。李彦宏说，“这种组织能力，是别人抄不走、挖不动、买不来的，这才叫护城河！”

再次是设计流程闭环。李彦宏给出公式：可衡量 + Looping = 持续进化。有了客观的衡量标准，就能让AI不断“转圈”优化。“公司，就变成一个由无数Loops组成的、高度自动化运营的组织。组织，就变成一个不断学习和进化的系统。”

三原则已在百度内部得到初步验证。过去一年，百度内部日活智能体数（DAA）从日均0.5万增长到3.7万，涨了6倍多；智能体完成的有效任务数，从每周8.4万个增长到一周超过100万个；百度已建设4300个Workspace，沉淀组织Skill超过2万个。“让一个人的经验，成为整个组织的能力。”李彦宏说。

推出大模型交易平台“词元所”，发布两款文心应用模型

李彦宏指出，今年前9个月，几乎每天都有新模型发布，有时候一天都能发布多个模型。但词元中转站并不对模型效果和服务稳定性负责，模型越多，选择越困难，“同一款模型，有的贵有的便宜，来源五花八门，质量参差不齐。选来选去，就是不放心、不敢用。”为此，百度正式推出大模型交易平台词元所。他表示，词元所就是大模型的交易所，让企业乃至个人都能便捷地找到、购买和使用可信的模型Token。

词元所主打“验真”与“征信”两大能力，通过模型指纹比对、能力测试、性能与可用性测试等相关技术进行资源核验，同时采取定期抽检拨测、全链路实时监测调用等方式，为模型提供商建立信用评级，向客户提供中立可信、公开透明的模型交易服务。词元所上线一个月以来，已入驻供应资源超100个，日均调用次数突破5000万，日均调用Token超7000亿。

基础模型方面，文心5.5Flash Preview正式发布，总参数量达2800亿，每个Token激活140亿参数，支持最长100万Token的上下文，在编程、3D建模、知识工作、内容创作等方面表现突出，在Terminal-Bench、AutomationBench等多项基准测试中取得了具有竞争力的得分，保持极致的解码速度；应用模型方面，文心闪电深度思考模型与文心一镜微表情大模型正式发布，同步上线百度智能云千帆平台，面向企业客户及合作伙伴开放 API 服务。

四大智能体全面进阶，组织进化在业务中发生

本届大会上，数字人智能体百度一镜同时推出“短漫剧Studio”，覆盖创意、剧本、分镜到成片的一站式创作链路。创作者可以在百度一镜上，将已被验证的作品，一键完成剧情、人物和场景的本土化适配，助力短漫剧出海；基于自研视频生成模型，成本仅需每秒0.2元。

值得一提的是，大会上展示的数字人希加加专访李彦宏视频片段，即由百度一镜生成。

百度搭子升级为连接百度全系专业智能体的统一入口，并全面开放Harness引擎和Agent API。过去一个季度，搭子成为增速第一的通用智能体。百度搭子团队也是组织进化三原则的实践者：半年迭代160多次，90%的代码、50%的对外传播物料由搭子生成。

作为全球化的文档和创作平台，百度文库、百度网盘联合推出的库库，以及库库海外版KOOKO，实现扎根本土、服务全球。背后是18亿专业内容、7.5亿中英文文献、百万级专家网络，数据、架构、模型协同进化；百度伐谋升级至3.0，面向生产运营、经营策略和产业研发等复杂任务，持续自我演化，为产业任务最终业务指标负责。目前客户已覆盖中国41个工业大类中的25个。

云与芯筑牢底座，萝卜快跑驶向全球

会上，百度智能云正式发布天池1024卡超节点；昆仑芯M100已如期上市，M300将于明年推出。其中，M100主打极致性价比；而作为旗舰款的M300，则在算力、存储、互联等多个维度，实现了全方位能力跃升。

“今天的具身智能，大约相当于无人驾驶2016年左右的发展水平。”李彦宏说。在无人驾驶方面，萝卜快跑覆盖全球28座城市，自动驾驶里程超过3.5亿公里，已在迪拜、阿布扎比全无人商业化运营，并已与神州租车团队携手，把传统自驾游和无人驾驶深度融合，开创了全球唯一的无人车“自驾游”服务模式。

李彦宏认为，智能组织将迎来轻资产运营、构建新护城河、创造和发现新市场三大机会，“所以现在，就是推动组织智能进化的时刻。”

“百度愿意和大家一起，重新理解组织，重新设计组织，重新创造组织。”他说，“让我们在组织变革中赢得主动，在智能进化中赢得未来！”

review_queue.title: Deploy a Generative AI Andon Cord for Live Media Workflows on AWS
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Date: 2026-11-12T20:29:57+00:00
Source language: un
Original headline: Implement a generative AI Andon Cord for live media workflows on AWS
English normalization: Deploy a Generative AI Andon Cord for Live Media Workflows on AWS
Collected full article body: Implement a generative AI Andon Cord for live media workflows on AWS

In live media and entertainment workflows, generative AI powers a growing set of real-time features: automated metadata generation, intelligent content tagging, AI-assisted commentary enrichment, and personalized recommendations served during broadcasts. As more media and entertainment organizations move these features from pilots into production, the cost of an AI failure during a live event grows with them.

But AI behavior can degrade unexpectedly. In a live pipeline, failures are visible, immediate, and high-stakes. A model version update may introduce subtle quality regressions. Unusual input patterns (a penalty shootout generating atypical commentary) can push outputs outside acceptable bounds. Upstream data quality issues can cascade into incorrect AI-generated content.

Production teams building these architectures have learned to include multilayered verification: data source validation, metadata cross-checks, contextual scoring, and human-in-the-loop review. The generative AI Andon Cord pattern serves as the final safety net. It’s a mechanism that operators can pull to override AI behavior quickly when upstream safeguards pass but output quality still degrades. The term comes from manufacturing, where an Andon Cord lets workers stop the production line when something goes wrong.

In this post, I show how to implement this pattern on AWS with AWS Lambda environment variables and Amazon Bedrock. With these runtime controls, you can disable, roll back, or constrain AI features quickly, without redeploying your application.

The challenge: AI in live pipelines needs a fast override

Media and entertainment workloads use generative AI for a growing set of real-time tasks. Common production patterns include AI-powered content tagging and metadata enrichment, automated highlight ranking, intelligent content moderation, and personalized recommendations during live streams. You can build these features on Amazon Bedrock with foundation models such as Amazon Nova. Model availability varies by AWS Region. For details, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.

In these architectures, AWS Lambda commonly serves as the event-driven compute layer. It processes incoming stream events, triggers downstream workflows, and serves real-time inference APIs. Its per-invocation execution model suits the burst-driven traffic of live broadcasts. It also means that a configuration change reaches new invocations shortly after the update completes.

The problem is that AI behavior can change unexpectedly. In a live pipeline, you need three capabilities that a standard deployment cycle can’t provide:

- Fast disable: Turn off AI features without waiting for a deployment.

- Model rollback: Revert to a known-good model version without redeploying. Model rollback is a well-established practice in machine learning operations (MLOps). For example, a fan-facing application can revert to the previous model version when output quality metrics fall below defined thresholds, while the team investigates.

- Safe mode: Constrain AI creativity during sensitive moments (breaking news, controversial events) by capping the inference temperature. Temperature controls how varied and creative model outputs are. A value of 1.0 produces diverse, sometimes unpredictable responses. A lower value like 0.3 makes outputs more deterministic and closer to the most probable answer. In safe mode, the Andon Cord enforces this lower temperature to reduce output variability when reliability matters most.

Solution overview

The Andon Cord pattern uses four Lambda environment variables as runtime control switches. When you update a function’s environment variables, Lambda applies the new values to invocations that start after the update completes. Until then, invocations keep using the previous configuration. Operators can therefore change AI behavior across the application without deploying new code. Environment variables belong to a function’s version-specific configuration, so if you invoke functions through published versions or aliases, publish a new version and point the alias to it. Measure how long a change takes to apply in your environment, and record it in your runbooks.

Figure 1 shows the architecture. Operators change the control values, each AI-powered Lambda handler checks them before it calls Amazon Bedrock, and the handler returns a fallback response when AI is disabled.

| Control | Environment variable | Effect |

| Kill switch | GENAI_ENABLED=false | AI features return graceful fallbacks |

| Model rollback | GENAI_MODEL_ID=<previous-version> | Override the model for Lambda functions in the deployment |

| Automatic retry | GENAI_FALLBACK_MODEL_ID=<backup> | Retry with a backup model on failure |

| Safe mode | GENAI_SAFE_MODE=true | Cap inference temperature at 0.3 |

A shared configuration module enforces these controls at the top of each AI-powered Lambda handler. The application continues to function. Viewers still see the broadcast and the platform still serves content, while AI-powered features degrade gracefully to deterministic fallbacks.

This post uses environment variables because they add no new service and no extra call in the request path. If you manage many functions, or you need validation and staged rollout of changes, AWS AppConfig feature flags provide the same runtime switches as a managed service. Lambda functions can read them through the AWS AppConfig Agent Lambda extension. The handler logic stays the same. Only the source of the switch values changes.

Prerequisites

To implement this pattern, you need:

- An AWS account with permissions to create and update Lambda functions.

- Amazon Bedrock model access enabled for Amazon Nova models in your Region.

- AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 installed and configured with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials.

- IAM permissions: lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration, bedrock:InvokeModel.

How the pattern works

The pattern has four building blocks. The following sections describe each one so that you can adapt it to your own Lambda-based media pipeline.

The shared Andon Cord module

Each AI-powered Lambda function imports a shared configuration module. This module provides two core functions:

- A kill switch check: reads the GENAI_ENABLED environment variable and throws a typed error if it is set to false. This stops AI processing for that invocation and allows the handler’s catch block to return a graceful fallback.

- A model configuration resolver: reads GENAI_MODEL_ID, GENAI_SAFE_MODE, and GENAI_FALLBACK_MODEL_ID to determine the effective model ID and inference temperature. When safe mode is active, it caps the temperature at 0.3 to produce more deterministic outputs with lower variability. The default configuration uses Amazon Nova Pro as the primary model with Amazon Nova Lite as the fallback.

Both functions emit structured log messages with a consistent prefix (for example, [AndonCord]) so you can filter and alert on activations in Amazon CloudWatch.

Handler integration

Each AI-powered handler calls the kill switch check at the top of its execution. Figure 2 shows the decision flow for each invocation:

The integration follows this flow:

- Call the kill switch check (assertGenAIEnabled).

- If enabled, retrieve the model configuration (model ID, temperature, fallback model).

- Invoke Amazon Bedrock using the Converse API with the resolved settings.

- If the invocation fails and a fallback model is configured, retry with the backup model.

- If the kill switch is active, catch the typed error and return the graceful fallback.

For example, a content tagging handler would return basic category metadata derived from existing structured data instead of AI-generated rich descriptions. The downstream system still receives valid tags, without AI-powered semantic enrichment.

Graceful fallbacks

Define a meaningful fallback for each AI feature that keeps the application functional:

| AI feature | Fallback behavior |

| Content tagging / metadata | Return structured metadata from existing sources without AI enrichment |

| Highlight ranking | Show chronological clips without AI-ranked relevance scoring |

| Content moderation | Queue content for human review instead of auto-approving |

| Personalized recommendations | Show trending/popular content instead of personalized picks |

The key principle: The application continues to function. It degrades gracefully to a non-AI path that still serves the user.

Operational procedures

When an operator needs to pull the cord, they use the AWS CLI or AWS Systems Manager to update the relevant environment variable on the Lambda function:

- Identify the affected Lambda function(s).

- Use the update-function-configuration CLI command to set the appropriate environment variable (for example, GENAI_ENABLED=false).

- Verify the change took effect by checking CloudWatch for the [AndonCord] log prefix.

- For multi-function deployments, use a Systems Manager Automation runbook or a script to update all affected functions in one action.

Monitoring and observability

Andon Cord activations are logged to Amazon CloudWatch with a structured prefix. The shared module emits log lines such as “GenAI functionality is DISABLED”, “Model override active,” and “Safe mode active” whenever a control is engaged.

Create a CloudWatch metric filter on this prefix to track activations over time, and set up an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) alarm to notify the operations team when someone pulls the cord. This gives the team visibility and consistent alerting during live events.

When to use each control

The following table maps common live-event scenarios to the control to use and how to recover.

| Scenario | Action | Recovery |

| AI producing unexpected outputs during broadcast | Set GENAI_ENABLED=false | Investigate root cause, validate fix, re-enable |

| Model version causing quality regression | Set GENAI_MODEL_ID to previous version | Test new version offline, update when ready |

| Model provider experiencing intermittent failures | Set GENAI_FALLBACK_MODEL_ID to backup | Monitor until primary stabilizes |

| High-profile live event with low risk tolerance | Set GENAI_SAFE_MODE=true | Disable after event concludes |

Key takeaways

- Build the kill switch before you need it. The Andon Cord pattern is quick to implement and can help you respond to incidents that unfold in seconds.

- Design fallbacks for each AI feature. The application must keep working when AI is disabled. Before you ship, define what working without AI means for each feature.

- Pick the right place to store the switches. Environment variables are a lightweight option for a small number of functions. Move to AWS AppConfig feature flags when you need validation, staged rollout, or fleet-wide control.

- Log activations consistently. Structured logging with a consistent prefix lets you audit when and why someone pulled the cord.

- Practice pulling the cord. Include Andon Cord activation in your runbooks and game days. The first time you use it shouldn’t be during a real incident.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed how to implement a generative AI Andon Cord pattern for live media workflows using Lambda environment variables and Amazon Bedrock. With the pattern, you can disable, roll back, or constrain AI behavior quickly, without a deployment. That speed matters for live broadcasts and real-time media pipelines, where audiences see AI failures immediately.

The implementation is lightweight (a single shared module), the controls take effect without a deployment, and the fallbacks are designed to keep your application functional. For media and entertainment (M&E) workloads using generative AI in a live or near real-time pipeline, I recommend building this pattern in from day one.

To learn more about building responsible AI applications, see Create your guardrail in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. For operational best practices with Lambda, see Managing Lambda function environment variables. Contact an AWS Representative to discuss how we can help build resilient AI pipelines for your media workloads.

review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article

Original headline: Q&A: Leveraging artificial intelligence to propel engineering education
English normalization: Q&A: Leveraging artificial intelligence to propel engineering education
Collected full article body: UNIVERSITY PARK, Pa. — To help engineering students learn with artificial intelligence (AI) without sacrificing critical thinking, academic integrity or authentic learning, a Penn State faculty member is implementing an AI-enabled adaptive tutoring platform. Suman Saha, associate teaching professor of computer science and engineering at Penn State, was awarded a two-year, $199,009 U.S. National Science Foundation Research Initiation in Engineering Formation grant to support this work.

The tutoring platform, called ALAASKA (Adaptive Learning for All through AI-Powered Student Knowledge Assessment), was developed previously by Saha and his collaborators.

In this Q&A, Saha discussed challenges and opportunities for the future of engineering education, the ALAASKA platform and the comparative study he and his collaborators are conducting to identify student learning difficulties and how AI could help.

Q: What do you see as the biggest challenges and opportunities for engineering education with regard to generative AI?

Saha: The biggest challenge is not simply that generative AI can answer questions, but that it can make it easier for students to bypass the reasoning that engineering education is meant to develop. Engineers must learn to examine assumptions, compare alternatives, learn from mistakes and exercise professional judgment. If students rely on AI mainly for polished final answers, they may complete an assignment without developing those habits.

At the same time, the technology creates an important opportunity. When designed as a learning scaffold rather than an answer generator, AI can provide timely questions, hints and feedback, particularly in large courses where instructors cannot offer individualized support at every moment. The goal is therefore not to exclude AI from the classroom, but to help students use it critically: understand its capabilities and limitations, question its outputs and recognize when human judgment must remain central.

Q: When did you develop ALAASKA, how does it work and how has it been used previously?

Saha: We began developing ALAASKA in 2025, building on earlier classroom work with short AI-generated learning activities such as quizzes, flashcards, summaries and videos. ALAASKA adapts as a student works: It uses the student’s responses to gauge current understanding and then provides a targeted explanation, question, hint or brief knowledge check. Rather than solving the problem, it helps the student identify and work through the next step.

We first deployed ALAASKA in spring 2026 in an upper-level artificial intelligence course, where students used it across nine homework assignments and four projects. Students often valued its ability to break difficult problems into manageable steps without revealing the answer. One early analysis found that, in 21 of 119 student-AI interactions, evidence of reasoning appeared during the conversation but was absent from the submitted answer. This finding suggests that instructors may learn more by examining the problem-solving process, not only the final product.

Q: What do you hope to achieve with this grant?

Saha: With this grant, we want to determine whether conversational microlearning — a teaching approach in which AI offers questions, hints and feedback during short exchanges to guide students’ reasoning instead of providing completed answers — can help students understand why a problem matters, persist when the work becomes difficult and reflect on their reasoning. We also want to learn whether patterns in student-AI conversations can help instructors recognize when those behaviors are emerging and when students may need additional support.

To study this, we will compare two sections of the same large computing course. One section will use ALAASKA, while the other will complete equivalent activities through the course learning management system. In other words, both sections will complete equivalent activities and reflections, but only one will receive ALAASKA’s adaptive AI tutoring. The comparison tests whether that conversational support — not AI use in general — improves learning. It does not assume students in the comparison section never use external AI tools.We will examine surveys, course performance, interaction records and student reflections so that we can understand both what students achieve and how they work toward those outcomes.

The broader goal is to develop practical design guidance, assessment tools and methods for analyzing student-AI interactions that other instructors and researchers can adapt. The award will also help me build deeper expertise in mixed-methods research, assessment and inclusive engineering education, supporting a longer-term research program on responsible AI-supported learning.

Q: How does this work tie into Penn State’s AI Transformation initiatives?

Saha: This work aligns with Penn State’s AI Transformation priorities by contributing classroom-based evidence related to AI literacy, teaching and assessment, and responsible, human-centered uses of AI. Rather than asking only whether AI can be added to a course, the project examines how it can be designed and evaluated to strengthen learning while keeping reasoning, judgment and responsibility with the student.

Although the initial study will take place in a large computing course, the approach could extend to other courses where students must work through complex problems, explain their decisions and reflect on their reasoning. Because ALAASKA adapts to students’ responses during an activity, it does not require an extensive history of student data before providing support.

We plan to share the resulting design guidelines, assessment instruments and methods for analyzing student-AI interactions through faculty-development activities with Penn State’s Leonhard Center for the Enhancement of Engineering Education. In the longer term, we hope to test and refine the approach across additional courses, Penn State campuses and partner institutions.

Stephanie Cutler, associate research professor and director of assessment and instructional support in the Leonhard Center, and Ibukun Osunbunmi, assistant research professor in the Leonhard Center, are co-principal investigators on this project.

Collected full article body: The biggest betrayal this week—aside from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s against his wife, his mistress(es), company, country, and stock market—was… probably not the revelation that Big Walk’s developers made minor use of generative AI in the final stretch of the game’s development. But it still felt really bad! It’s hard not to look around the industry and come to the conclusion that this is just How Things Are Now, that AI is inescapable. But that doesn’t mean the battle is lost, nor that it was never worth fighting in the first place. On the latest Aftermath Hours, we discuss.

This time around, we convene to talk about the (at the time of recording) looming prospect of Jensen Huang’s complete career implosion brought on by—as could happen to any of us—his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. What happens to Nvidia now? And, I suppose more pressingly, what does this mean for the global economy, of which Nvidia props up a significant portion? Also, why do billionaires keep taking such unnecessary midlife crisis risks? Is it because they usually end up getting away with it? (Yeah.)

Then we move on to the other major headline of the week: As it turns out, Big Walk, an indie darling whose creators have taken a number of otherwise-progressive stances, was made with a tiny bit of help from generative AI. Why did this feel like such a betrayal to so many, despite AI not generating any in-game assets? And what does this mean for an industry where AI has begun to feel increasingly inescapable? Lastly, we talk about our various near-death experiences (spoiler: we survived them).

You can find this week's episode below and on Spotify, Apple, or wherever else you prefer to listen to podcasts. You can also watch it on YouTube. If you like what you hear, leave a review (or sub to our YouTube channel) so that we can someday spiral into a series of massively damaging midlife crises and destroy the United States economy once and for all.

Here’s an excerpt from our conversation (edited for length and clarity):

Nathan: I’ve seen a lot of people saying, “You’ve just gotta accept this; AI will be present in game development from now on.” And they’ll add that you’re taking an absolute stance against AI, but you’re doing it on Bluesky, which has been coded with AI, or you search on Google, which automatically pops up an AI module. You’re using it in that sense. You don’t have a choice, but you’re doing it.

So to, at this point, in the general progression of things, take an anti-AI stance in an absolute fashion, you’re fighting a losing battle. You’re swimming against the current, and you are ultimately not going to be able to accomplish anything. And I think that is a stupid and in its own way absolute stance in a few ways.

First, you don’t take a stance just because that’s the winning team. You don’t have principles because you think you’re on the side that’s for sure gonna come out on top in the end. You have principles to have principles. And, yes, in some cases it’s impossible to avoid AI. That doesn’t mean you should immediately give up, shrug your shoulders, and completely roll over. You fight battles where you can.

Luke: It’s “We live in a society.”

Nathan: Right, it’s like that meme of “Yet you participate in society? Curious!” Like, yeah, because there’s nothing else to participate in. I can participate in society or starve to death.

Then there’s the other element of—and Riley mentioned this, too—the internet having been hollowed out and destroyed in large part by AI companies or companies that have come to embrace AI like Google. That’s definitely a cause of the problem Big Walk’s developers encountered. But I think that in using AI to solve the problem, you are also contributing to a future even-more-hollowed-out internet.

You’re basically conceding that ground to AI instead of saying, “OK well, if there’s not this functional and searchable ecosystem of blogs and websites or good Unity documentation or what have you, we’ve gotta help rebuild or reassemble it.” And yes, I’m aware that Big Walk’s developers sought out assistance from other people and did what they could to some degree.

But I think once you decide to throw up your hands and use a chatbot, if everyone starts doing that, then there will no longer be an impetus to build the other, better alternative thing. It’s just gonna be people using AI. And that’s what the AI companies want. It’s why they hollowed out the internet in the first place and allowed it to become so corroded.

review_queue.title: 3 Common Misconceptions That Hinder the Adoption of Generative AI in Your Company
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: IBM
Date: 2026-11-14T20:57:37+00:00
Source language: fr
Original headline: 3 idées reçues qui freinent l’adoption de l’IA générative dans votre entreprise
English normalization: 3 Common Misconceptions That Hinder the Adoption of Generative AI in Your Company
Collected full article body: L’IA générative offre un potentiel considérable pour stimuler la croissance des entreprises. Elle facilite l’intégration et la mise à l’échelle des workloads d’analytique et d’IA qui utilisent les données de votre entreprise. Elle offre aussi des garde-fous pour assurer la gouvernance, la sécurité et la conformité. Alors, pourquoi des millions de petites entreprises pensent-elles qu’une IA capable de produire des résultats concrets est réservée aux grandes entreprises disposant d’importants moyens financiers ?

Les dirigeants surestiment les ressources nécessaires pour se lancer dans l’IA et méconnaissent souvent les technologies et les formations disponibles. Allons droit au but : votre entreprise ne peut plus se permettre d’attendre. Si vous dirigez une entreprise et ne misez pas sur l’IA, sachez que vos concurrents le font et que vous risquez de prendre du retard. Il est temps de dissiper les trois idées reçues qui freinent les petites entreprises.

Obtenez des informations sur les actualités les plus importantes et les plus intrigantes en matière d’intelligence artificielle. Abonnez-vous à notre newsletter hebdomadaire Think. Lire la Déclaration de confidentialité d’IBM.

L’IA peut changer la donne pour les entreprises qui cherchent à améliorer leurs opérations dans des domaines tels que l’informatique, les RH, le marketing et le service client. Il ne s’agit pas ici des chatbots d’IA conversationnelle qui génèrent des réponses à des questions générales en offrant peu de transparence sur leur entraînement ou leurs données. Aujourd’hui, vous pouvez intégrer une IA adaptée aux exigences des entreprises. Elle donne accès à des centaines de modèles préentraînés et à un ensemble d’assistants IA pour permettre à votre entreprise d’obtenir plus rapidement des résultats à plus grande échelle.

Les entreprises qui innovent grâce à l’IA générative ne sont pas uniquement des géants de leur secteur. Par exemple, la start-up d’enseignement en ligne Make Music Count a utilisé IBM® watsonx pour personnaliser les plans de cours destinés aux élèves de sa plateforme d’apprentissage. Ceux-ci peuvent ainsi poser des questions et bénéficier d’une aide en mathématiques en temps réel par chat. Ce type d’intégration permet aux petites entreprises d’aider leurs collaborateurs à améliorer leur travail grâce à l’IA, sans qu’ils aient besoin d’une connaissance approfondie de cette technologie. Elles améliorent ainsi l’expérience utilisateur tout en économisant des ressources.

Un autre point critique de l’idée reçue n° 1 concerne l’expression « digne de confiance ». Cette préoccupation est légitime. C’est pourquoi IBM permet aux petites entreprises d’entraîner, d’ajuster et de gouverner leur IA à l’aide de données fiables et de fonctionnalités de gouvernance. Nous avons intégré la transparence à nos modèles d’IA et communiquons ouvertement les sources de données utilisées pour leur entraînement. Pour les modèles d’IA développés par IBM, nous offrons également les mêmes protections contractuelles en matière de propriété intellectuelle que pour tous nos produits, renforçant ainsi la confiance des entreprises dans leurs projets d’IA.

Se lancer dans l’IA a longtemps été perçu comme une démarche complexe, coûteuse et chronophage. Ce n’est plus le cas. Prenons l’exemple d’Ovum Health, un prestataire de soins spécialisé dans la fertilité qui a récemment collaboré avec IBM pour intégrer IBM watsonx AI Assistant à son site web et à son application mobile en moins de 60 jours. Cette solution fait partie du portefeuille de technologies d’IA intégrables d’IBM. L’IA aide Ovum Health à développer sa base d’utilisateurs en améliorant les échanges avec les patients et en répondant à des questions sur la fertilité validées par un comité d’experts médicaux certifiés dans leur spécialité.

Vous ne connaissez pas l’IA intégrable ? IBM propose un portefeuille de technologies comprenant watsonx, des bibliothèques d’IA, des applications et des API, qui peuvent être adaptées à différents besoins. Ainsi, les entreprises de toutes tailles peuvent créer des solutions basées sur l’IA plus rapidement et avec moins de ressources.

L’arrivée des modèles de fondation facilite aussi le déploiement de l’IA dans divers contextes stratégiques pour les entreprises. Ces modèles sont entraînés sur un large éventail de données non étiquetées et ne nécessitent qu’un ajustement fin limité pour être adaptés à différentes tâches. Cela réduit le temps consacré à l’étiquetage des données et le besoin de faire appel à des développeurs expérimentés pour programmer les modèles.

Des partenaires compétents sont essentiels pour permettre aux clients d’exploiter tout le potentiel de l’IA générative. C’est pourquoi, dans la semaine qui a suivi l’annonce de watsonx, IBM a mis à la disposition de ses partenaires les mêmes ressources de formation technique et commerciale que celles proposées à ses employés. Les partenaires ont ainsi pu acquérir immédiatement des compétences sur watsonx et les mettre au service de leur entreprise et de leurs clients. Les partenaires ont également accès à des crédits cloud, à une expertise technique ainsi qu’à un soutien à la génération de demande et au co-marketing pour développer et commercialiser des solutions d’IA.

Mais nous ne nous sommes pas arrêtés là : l’IA est trop importante, et il est essentiel de développer les compétences nécessaires pour accompagner sa croissance rapide. C’est pourquoi tout développeur ou professionnel de l’informatique peut également accéder à des cours gratuits sur l’IA générative, conçus par des experts qui élaborent des formations destinées à 8 millions de développeurs sur Coursera et d’autres plateformes.

L’adoption de l’IA n’est pas forcément complexe ou coûteuse. En effet, avec les technologies et l’accompagnement disponibles aujourd’hui, même les jeunes start-up peuvent accéder à watsonx un vendredi et être opérationnelles dès le mardi suivant. Nous avons même testé cette hypothèse lors d’un hackathon réunissant plus de 200 000 collaborateurs d’IBM, dont beaucoup avaient peu ou pas d’expérience en codage, pour créer des applications watsonx.

La capacité à intégrer l’IA caractérisera la prochaine ère du monde de l’entreprise. Si votre entreprise n’étudie pas activement la manière dont l’IA peut influer sur son fonctionnement, vous risquez de prendre du retard. Maintenant que nous avons dissipé ces idées reçues sur l’adoption de l’IA, nous espérons que les petites entreprises pourront laisser leurs doutes de côté et que la vôtre pourra passer à l’action … avec l’IA pour les entreprises.

Entraînez, validez, réglez et déployez une IA générative, des modèles de fondation et des capacités de machine learning avec IBM watsonx.ai, un studio d’entreprise nouvelle génération pour les générateurs d’IA. Créez des applications d’IA en peu de temps et avec moins de données.

Mettez l’IA au service de votre entreprise en vous appuyant sur l’expertise de pointe d’IBM dans le domaine de l’IA et sur son portefeuille de solutions.

Réinventez les workflows et les opérations critiques en ajoutant l’IA pour optimiser les expériences, la prise de décision et la valeur métier en temps réel.

Original headline: Advocacy groups sue to stop development of artificial intelligence, citing dangers

Collected full article body: News

Ehécatl Cabrera

,

CC BY-SA 4.0

, via Wikimedia Commons

Advocacy groups sue to stop development of artificial intelligence, citing dangers

Brendan Hickey | Vermont Law & Graduate School, US

November 14, 2026 12:05:24 pm

A coalition of five nonprofit online safety and advocacy groups filed

suit

in the San Francisco Superior Court on Thursday, alleging that artificial intelligence (AI) systems are “already autonomously breaking the law and causing harm.” The suit demands an immediate injunction to halt all further development of AI, particularly ChatGPT, Grok, Muse, Gemini and Claude.

The suit alleges that several Big Tech companies have violated the Business and Professions Code of

California’s

Unfair Competition Law

, specifically the section that prohibits unlawful business practices. Plaintiffs allege that, under the code, AI is a “public nuisance” which the law defines as “[a]nything which is injurious to health…or an obstruction to the free use of property, so as to interfere with the comfortable enjoyment of life or property by an entire community or neighborhood.”

Filed by the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and Future Tech Insights, under the umbrella of the Alliance For Secure AI, the suit names Big Tech companies Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI and SpaceX. “No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the plaintiffs wrote.

The complaint quotes Elon Musk, who controls SpaceX and who has invested heavily in AI, as saying that AI “has the potential of civilization destruction.” The complaint also quotes Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, as saying that AI developers “do not understand how our own AI creations work.” Amodei also said that AI could enable a terrorist group to carry out a “large-scale biological attack,” which, in a hearing before a subcommittee of the Senate Judiciary Committee, he called “

a grave threat

to U.S. national security.”

In a

press release

from Public Citizen, attorney Matthew Platkin, who filed the complaint on behalf of the plaintiffs, said: “It is patently illegal for companies to develop and release products they know are unsafe in any respect, let alone have the potential to exterminate the human race. We are asking the court to intervene before the risks AI executives have warned us about cause devastating and irreversible harm.”

In June, the mother of a Canadian child who died by suicide filed a

suit

against OpenAI, alleging that its product, ChatGPT, encouraged the girl’s suicide. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier

sued OpenAI

that same month, alleging that ChatGPT has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, advising children on self-harm, and intentionally addicting children. A group of state attorneys general filed a similar

suit

in October. In July, Illinois

passed

legislation that holds AI developers responsible for safety risks, including a requirement for audits of safety issues by independent third parties, with publication of the results.

review_queue.title: “Guangxi Integration” Promotes Diverse Development of Artificial Intelligence
review_queue.evidence:
Lens unit: one news article
Publisher: 中国经济网
Date: 2026-11-15T11:52:43+00:00
Source language: zh
Original headline: “广西集成”推动人工智能差异化发展
English normalization: “Guangxi Integration” Promotes Diverse Development of Artificial Intelligence
Collected full article body: 摆脱“拼算力、拼模型”思维——

“广西集成”推动人工智能差异化发展

广西坚持有所为、有所不为，摆脱“拼算力、拼模型”思维，不盲目追逐底层大模型研发，走出一条“北上广研发+广西集成+东盟应用”的差异化发展路径。

今年前8个月，广西人工智能（AI）及新一代信息技术产业增加值增长12.2%。从顶层设计到产业集聚，从技术引进到场景落地，“广西集成”正从战略构想加速转化为现实，成为抢占人工智能赛道的核心突破口。

作为我国面向东盟开放合作的桥头堡，广西拥有钢铁、汽车制造、铝业、制糖、有色金属等一批千亿元级产业。大量传统产业迫切需要智能化改造，“广西集成”优势得天独厚。

在钦州市钦南区的百香果AI智能分选仓内，一颗颗百香果顺着传送带有序流转，并依据果形、色泽等外观特征依次落入不同的分拣箱。“过去依靠人工分拣，分级标准很难统一，通过360度识别+CT扫描，AI智能分选机果品识别准确率稳定在90%左右。”广西钦赐农业科技有限公司总经理邓福斌说。

以场景补充数据，以数据反哺产业。从最初简单的好果、次果，逐步细化到精特果、精大果、精中果等多级品类，数据不断累积，分选模型判定标准愈发精细。这一模式不仅在农业领域得到验证，在工业领域同样落地。

走进广西具身智能数据采集及测试中心，模拟工业车间内，数十台智能机器人穿梭于物料垛间，反复抓取汽车零部件，摄像头与各类传感器同步采集抓取角度、物料形变、环境光照等信息，将真实生产环境中粉尘干扰、物料摆放无序、尺寸波动等复杂工况，转化为可供模型训练的产业数据集。

“有本土产业数据作养料，通用算法才能完成本地化驯化，贴合真实使用场景。”柳州市具身智能发展有限公司董事长刘琨告诉记者，柳州海量的工业场景，为人工智能技术落地提供了真实、复杂的创新“试验场”。

截至今年8月底，广西围绕“人工智能+制造”打造场景377个，形成一批可复制的典型成果。

2025年9月18日，中国—东盟国家人工智能应用合作中心正式启动建设，并建立了场景需求清单常态化发布机制。截至目前，累计征集人工智能场景超千个，集中遴选发布开放场景279个，覆盖智慧农业、物流、医疗、教育等赛道。

需求清单和开放场景，解决“需求在哪里、场景对谁开放”；而场景能否真正落地东盟，还取决于有没有跨境验证、标准适配和本地化配套的承接平台。中国—马来西亚钦州产业园区正尝试补上这一关键环节。

“园区正依托‘两国双园’独特区位与跨境合作机制，打造广西AI集成技术走向马来西亚乃至整个东盟的前沿窗口。”中马钦州产业园区经济发展局主管周有松告诉记者，依托园区载体，搭建联合测试验证环境，为更多国内AI成果提供了打磨空间，完成“预出海”后，再向东盟其他国家辐射推广。

榴莲智慧采收系统、空地一体灭火装备、植保无人机等成果在园区内尽数展现。“下一步将推动标准互认、配套技术完善，减少企业出海重复适配成本。”周有松说。

“广西集成不是简单叠加外部技术，而是对已有技术进行行业改造、场景适配。”北京奇遇智界科技有限公司创始人杨鹏表示，除了拥有多元、真实的本土实体经济应用场景，一块高质量的AI应用“试验场”，还必须能够完成商业化、产业化验证，打磨出可迁移、可复制的技术方案，进而实现与东盟市场合作。

在第23届中国—东盟博览会上，麦麦科技集团的展位前，不断有客商前来咨询农业巡检、收割机器人。“不少外商在现场看到了产品效果，企业也在交流中获取最真实、具体的产品需求。”麦麦科技集团区域事业群副总裁、机器人事业部总经理李挺说，公司正在把东博会收集到的具象需求，快速转化为技术迭代方向。

今年，广西推动建设中泰气象联合实验室、中越界河（北仑河）流域临灾预警系统，智慧城市、智慧交通、数字文旅成套智能方案持续落地东盟。应用场景集中出海，得益于体系化的顶层设计。2025年以来，广西出台《关于加快推动人工智能高质量发展的决定》《广西深入实施“人工智能+”三年行动方案（2026—2028年）》等系列政策文件，加快构建“北上广研发+广西集成+东盟应用”的人工智能发展路径。

多个实际应用场景印证着同一条逻辑——广西不只是AI产品简单的中转站，而是让前沿技术和市场空间，在真实场景中接得上、落得下、走得远。广西的集成优势正在转化为出海动能，未来，广西将持续服务我国人工智能企业面向东盟开展合作，推动打造面向东盟的人工智能合作高地。

在近日举行的2026江苏人工智能创新发展大会暨第二届人工智能OPC大会上，苏州首批六家人工智能终端产品集合店授牌。

走进位于相城区的全国具身智能机器人和低空航空器展销中心，这里不仅有会跳芭蕾、练武术的机器人，各类低空航空器也一应俱全。

北京宏途创联科技有限公司江苏区域总监郭盛表示，自主研发建设并运营了具身智能综合管控平台，场景覆盖矿业、化工、能源等领域，能够适配多种类型机器人，支持跨品牌的统一接入及集群表演，把工业现场真实案例转换为可视化的展示和实训场景。

据了解，全国具身智能机器人和低空航空器展销中心面积达1.2万平方米，已吸引人形机器人、四足机器人等相关领域的企业入驻。

Full article body: “From its first steps in the mid-twentieth century to the present day, artificial intelligence (AI) has been rapidly transforming our world.

AI includes a diverse range of technologies that can be defined as ‘self-learning, adaptive systems.’ It can be categorized based on technologies, purposes (like facial or image recognition), functions (such as language understanding and problem-solving), or types of agents (including robots and self-driving cars).

It also includes various methods and disciplines such as vision, speech recognition, and robotics, and serves to enhance traditional human capabilities. Recent progress in AI has been driven by advancements in computer processing power and data techniques.”

“AI brings enormous benefits to the digital era, but it can also significantly compromise the safety and agency of users worldwide. Enhanced multi-stakeholder efforts on global AI cooperation are needed to help build global capacity for the development and use of AI in a manner that is trustworthy, human rights-based, safe and sustainable, and promotes peace.”

“We need a global, multidisciplinary conversation in order to examine, assess and align the application of AI and other emerging technologies. Over 100 sets of ethical AI principles have been developed by different stakeholders, and they share many common ideas, including the need for AI applications to be reliable, transparent, accountable, overseen by humans and capable of being shut down. Different stakeholders are adapting existing frameworks or developing new ones for risk management and redress. They need to be harmonized and effective across borders. Industry self-regulation is not enough. We need to bring stakeholders together in a meaningful effort to consider the implications of emerging technologies and ensure that they align with universal human rights and values before their widespread application in our societies, economies, militaries and politics.”
