Because SB 53 requires OES to revoke a designation if the relevant criteria are no longer met, it may wish to establish the procedures through which it will ensure the continued effectiveness of the federal standard. This might involve a regular review process, public notice of California’s reconsideration, and the opportunity for the public to submit data and reviews to OES.371 Establishing such a process in advance may also have the benefit of avoiding any perception that California is singling out a particular federal standard for political reasons.

Incident reporting is only one slice of SB 53. California officials implementing SB 53 may nonetheless take account of developments in other jurisdictions by crafting guidance and implementing requirements in a manner designed to harmonize relevant standards to the greatest extent permitted by the law, without diluting its goals.

More generally, if the broader “trust but verify” approach to AI governance succeeds at the state level, there will be a strong case for federalizing it. Each of the relevant factors counsels in favor of a federal approach. A single set of rules requiring developers to create and adhere to frontier AI safety frameworks would minimize the compliance burden on industry without sacrificing safety. Consumers and citizens have little need for such rules to be tailored to local preferences, as identical foundation models are served by a small handful of companies nationwide. At the same time, federalizing safety and reporting requirements would strengthen the work of federal evaluation bodies, especially CAISSI.

Federal expertise will also be essential. States, including California, are working to bring technical experts into government to oversee AI governance, but, as is outlined earlier in this report, the talent necessary to understand frontier AI capabilities, inform policy, and design mitigations is in short supply. Duplicating this effort across many different states will be far less efficient than creating centralized sources of expertise at the federal level.

Although unifying the “trust but verify” approach at the federal level would bring gains in efficiency, when it comes to some elements, such as whistleblower protections, the case for federal leadership is less apparent. Whistleblowing channels exist at both the state and federal levels, after all, and collecting such reports may not require the same level of expertise as frontier model evaluation. If states create successful systems, disrupting them may be costly.

SB 53 is a state law, but the questions it raises are national and even global. California acted because it has a responsibility to its citizens, and because the federal government has not yet set rules for the frontier developers whose models will shape the economy, public safety, and national security in the years ahead.

But acting first is not the same as acting alone. SB 53’s designation provision reflects the reality that the federal-state division of labor over AI will change as the federal government develops its approach. Such provisions can help smooth the handoff between state and federal governance. Many aspects of frontier AI are likely well suited to federal intervention, thanks to the national nature of the market for foundation models, the national security implications of transformative AI, and the need for regulatory expertise. The designation mechanism thus creates a standing offer: Once the federal government can adopt an effective incident reporting standard of its own, California is positioned to step back.

That approach is a model other states can use. New York and Illinois have both adopted frontier AI governance laws—the RAISE Act and SB 315—that parallel many aspects of SB 53, and SB 315 goes further by establishing interoperability with certain other regulatory regimes. If more states follow suit, analogous designation provisions may give any eventual federal standard a clear path to creating a uniform national rule. By precommitting to the conditions under which they will defer to federal authority, states can both reduce the risk of conflicting rules and demonstrate to federal policymakers what a workable, credible standard looks like. SB 53 will not be the last word in the federal-state conversation over frontier AI governance; it is an early move in a longer process.

The technologies that emerge from California will reshape how communities and societies operate around the United States and the world. Frontier AI is no exception. Governance ideas that have emerged in California will shape how companies with truly global reach operate; entities from all over the world have become part of a dynamic ecosystem that enables compliance with California’s law.

Whether SB 53 creates its designed impact will depend on a series of implementation choices now in front of California policymakers. The standards California sets for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, and the disclosure of internal deployments will determine whether “trust but verify” frameworks generate meaningful evidence and transparency. Decisions around incident reporting—what counts as a reportable incident, what information must be reported, and what the state does with reports once they arrive—will shape whether the state enables meaningful situational awareness. The whistleblower channels being built now will determine whether SB 53’s transparency measures will actually create accountability. Ultimately, these early implementation design choices will create path dependencies that shape future AI laws. Getting these decisions right—in California and in every jurisdiction that follows its lead—is of the utmost importance.

SB 53 is global in nature because its subject, frontier AI development, is global, and because the verification ecosystem it relies on—UK AISI, U.S. CAISSI, and independent third-party evaluators distributed across institutions—is necessarily transnational. Many of the law’s foundational components, such as frontier AI frameworks and scoping coverage, are explicitly grounded in both national and international standards, and ideas about these standards are being developed through global conversations. When companies demonstrate how they comply with frontier AI frameworks through transparency reports, they often do so by voluntarily submitting their models for testing not just to U.S. CAISSI but also to UK AISI. Other countries around the world—such as Australia, Canada, China, France, India, Japan, Singapore, and South Korea—have followed these examples and are building institutional capacity inside or closely connected to the government to understand and manage different AI risks. When one jurisdiction has a powerful idea in AI governance, others follow. The close mirroring of the RAISE Act and SB 315 to SB 53 highlights a pathway toward national harmonization and even global consensus: replicating the core parts of the paradigm while leaving sufficient space to tailor to local constituent needs.

California offers a domestic foundation for what will inevitably need to be a global effort to manage AI’s risks. “Trust but verify” only works fully when frontier developers’ employees, wherever they sit, have credible channels to surface evidence of catastrophic risk. California cannot create those channels outside its borders, but the protections it establishes inside them as well as the requirements it puts on companies doing business within the state set a template that other jurisdictions can adopt. The same logic applies to the rest of the paradigm: So long as they have no system to receive critical incident reports occurring within their borders, governments will lack both situational awareness and the ability to share an appropriate amount of information across borders. International AI risk management will bring unique security and legal challenges, but it begins with each country developing its own domestic, interoperable risk management infrastructures.

The model- and developer-level interventions SB 53 creates make the world safer. However, they are one part of a broader effort for global AI security. Misuse, malicious adaptation, and the harms that emerge only at the point of application sit downstream of those interventions and will require complementary measures by the jurisdictions where deployment occurs. Other jurisdictions will need to be part of a global, interconnected risk management effort that weaves model-level interventions with those downstream of AI developers. Well-developed “trust but verify” policies offer a foundation upon which these other efforts can build.

Every government has a stake in how California governs frontier AI because the technologies emerging from California will touch their citizens. The path toward the best outcomes is narrow, and the stakes are high. The choices California makes today will shape the future of frontier AI governance for decades to come.

Original headline: What May Artificial Intelligence Do for Writers? (updated)
English normalization: What Can Artificial Intelligence Do for Writers? (updated)
Full article body: When it comes to permissible uses of AI in professional writing, one philosopher argues that “anything that is acceptable to ask a human to do is, other things equal, acceptable for an LLM to do. (Equivalently, anything it would be wrong to ask a human to do is wrong to ask an LLM to do.)”

This “simple principle” was put forward by Kyle van Oosterum (Southampton) at his newsletter, Unchambered, several months ago.

The principle rules out, van Oosterum says, having an LLM write an article for you and you failing to acknowledge that. Writers are generally not morally permitted to “take credit for someone else’s work,” and that goes not just when the someone else is a someone but also when it is a something . But the principle doesn’t prohibit, he says, using an AI to “transcribe interviews, generate pushback on my… thesis, suggest trims when I’m over my word count, sharpen podcast interview questions, and perform a final fact check on columns and editorials.”

van Oosterum says:

The Simple Principle would, therefore, permit [a writer] to use an LLM to complete the very same tasks which are ‘ancillary’ to the main job. This point is crucial. The principle is compatible with the obviously-true idea that an author retains ultimate responsibility; just as one cannot blame a human assistant for a published error, the author remains the agent responsible for the final output.

Is van Oosterum’s principle a good one? The idea is to piggyback on the existing norms we have regarding authorship and assistance.

Keep in mind it was offered in something like blog post. Presumably, he would sharpen it up some were it to appear in a less casual venue. We can do a little of that work. Here is the original version again:

1. Anything that is acceptable to ask a human to do is, other things equal, acceptable for an LLM to do. (Equivalently, anything it would be wrong to ask a human to do is wrong to ask an LLM to do.)

To start, the language of “asking” is a distraction; the principle is supposed to be about the ethics of having AIs and other people complete tasks for you, not the ethics of asking them to do so. (Which is not to say that there might not be interesting ethical questions about asking.)

Now let’s turn to the ceteris paribus clause. I’m not quite sure what “other things equal” is supposed to refer to in the context of this principle. It can’t mean “provided no other possibly morally relevant issues besides the bare assigning of the task to a human or an LLM arise,” for what we’re interested in, when assessing the principle, is whether there are other morally relevant issues that tend to arise with this choice that it doesn’t adequately address. So I’m tempted to leave it out, and simply say that whatever results from our further refinement may be a defeasible principle.

Next, note that the parenthetical van Oosterum added to the principle (Equivalently…”) implies he meant it as a biconditional. Put in a form that makes that clear, and taking into account the other revisions, we get the following principle:

2. For professional writing, it is morally permissible to have an AI/LLM perform a writing-related task if and only if it is permissible to have a human perform that task.

What do you think?

A few preliminaries:

- The principle is being offered up for our consideration. That it may conflict with the extant policies of journals and other publications is beside the point.

- Humans and AIs have different capacities; each may be able to do things (or do things in certain ways, or for certain durations) that the other cannot. Does that matter for this principle? No. The principle is about permitted acts, not required ones. While ‘ought’ implies ‘can,’ ‘may’ does not.

- The principle is presumably intended for AIs/LLMs roughly as they are now. If their capacities significantly change, so too may the principle(s) that apply to it.

- That an act is morally permissible is not necessarily the only morally relevant thing to say about it.

Is this a good way to approach the ethics of authorship in the era of AI? Discussion welcome.

UPDATE: A reader draws my attention to a substantively similar principle put forward by Mark Robert Taylor (Calvin University) in an article published in January in the Journal of Philosophy of Education. In “The Obligation to Restrict AI in Student Writing” (PhilPapers link) Taylor says:

I am arguing against only those uses of AI which, were they performed by a person, such as a student’s classmate, would violate the academic values which forbid plagiarism. If a student is permitted to talk over essay ideas with a classmate, she ought to be permitted to discuss the same with AI. On the other hand, if a student is not permitted to submit an outline which her classmate wrote, she should not be permitted to submit an outline which was AI generated. If a student consults with an AI for ideas or actual phrasing, as she would a secondary source, this may be appropriate but only if the AI is properly cited in the way a secondary source must be. In other words, teachers ought, pragmatically, to treat student use of AI as they would student dependence on other people. My central contention is that teachers who allow students to use AI in cases where they would forbid dependence on other persons are in a position morally parallel to allowing plagiarism.

Taylor also discusses the article in a post at New Work in Philosophy.

English normalization: A international center dedicated to defense artificial intelligence will open in France
Full article body: Ce jeudi, le ministère des Armées a présenté le prochain centre international pour l’IA de défense. Il devrait être opérationnel l’été prochain du côté de Rennes. La France souhaite mettre en place de nouvelles pratiques qui permettront d’améliorer les compétences des armées.

L’IA s’invite dans les opérations militaires

Nous parlons souvent de l’intelligence artificielle dans les entreprises, mais elle se déploie aussi dans les opérations militaires. L’objectif consiste à améliorer la planification des missions, à collecter des renseignements ou encore à optimiser les opérations. Les armées pourront ainsi améliorer leurs compétences en s’appuyant sur l’IA.

Le directeur adjoint de l’Agence ministérielle pour l’intelligence artificielle de défense (AMIAD), le contre-amiral Vincent Sébastien, révèle que tous « ceux qui prétendent aujourd’hui à la puissance militaire s’en sont saisis ».

Pourquoi ce centre international est-il si important ?

Selon la présentation faite à Rennes par le ministère des Armées, il doit structurer une communauté de travail. Cette dernière sera basée sur l’intelligence artificielle et aura pour objectif de partager des retours d’expérience. Ce sera aussi l’occasion d’optimiser le déploiement de l’IA dans les armées. Ce projet n’est pas récent : il s’inscrit dans la stratégie ministérielle présentée en mars 2024.

Elle a permis de créer l’AMIAD en mai 2024, qui travaille à l’intégration des capacités d’IA. À l’inverse, l’ICAID favorisera la coopération internationale. C’est Sébastien Lecornu qui avait proposé la création d’un tel centre en s’inspirant de celui dédié à la cyberdéfense.

Pour le gouvernement, les armées doivent se former rapidement au déploiement de l’IA afin de ne pas retarder leur montée en compétences.

Qui sera accueilli dans le centre ?

34 personnes devraient rejoindre ce centre ; il y aura des militaires et des civils. La France enverra 17 personnes et plusieurs alliés se sont déjà engagés dans ce projet. Ce centre sera basé à Rennes et ce choix est stratégique. En effet, la ville accueille déjà la DGA, le ComCyber ainsi que le Commissariat au numérique de défense.

Plusieurs missions sont déjà prévues :

- Animer une communauté d’intérêt.

- Favoriser l’adoption de l’IA.

- Développer les bonnes pratiques.

- Assurer une veille technologique.

- Centraliser les retours d’expérience.

Le contre-amiral révèle que le centre ne sera pas dédié à la production de services IA. Il s’agira d’un lieu de travail intellectuel avec des simulations, des hackathons et des benchmarks. Un premier hackathon est d’ailleurs organisé avec l’École du train et de la logistique par l’AMIAD.

Full article body: Manchester Animation Festival (MAF), the UK’s only Oscar® and BAFTA®‑qualifying animation festival, has unveiled the winners of its 2026 Film Competition, Industry Excellence Awards and MAFter Dark programme, recognising outstanding achievement across the international animation industry.

Presented at the Festival’s annual awards ceremony, hosted by writer, comedian and actor Molly McGuinness, the awards honoured excellence across British Film, Feature Film, Short Film, Student Film, Commissioned Film, Immersive Work, Children’s Shorts and the Audience Award. The ceremony also recognised exceptional contributions to the art and craft of animation through the Industry Excellence Awards, spanning writing, storyboarding, character design and character animation. Alongside these honours, MAF hosted the Young Animator of the Year Awards, celebrating emerging talent aged 11-22.

In a landmark move for the animation sector, Manchester Animation Festival has also announced today that films created using generative AI will no longer be accepted for submission from 2027 onwards. The new policy reflects the Festival’s commitment to celebrating human creativity and safeguarding the artistic skills that sit at the heart of animation.

After a whirlwind week celebrating the international animation community with screenings, panels, masterclasses and more, our awards are a wonderful way to reflect on the skills and talent we champion at MAF. As we open our call for entries for MAF 2027 we wanted to stand by the creatives that make animation the incredible, human artform that it is. Our new Gen AI policy puts artists first and continues our mission to showcase the very best animation has to offer making it clear for audiences and artists where MAF stands on Gen AI.

Steve Henderson, Festival Director

This year the Feature Film Award went to In Waves (Belgium, France, US), directed by Phuong Mai Nguyen. A Special Mention was awarded to We Are Aliens (Japan, France), directed by Kōhei Kadowaki. The Short Film Award was presented to When the Sea Was Calm (Georgia), directed by Mamuka Tkeshelashvili, with a Special Mention going to Anna Ginsburg’s Hag (UK). The Best British Short Award was awarded to A Little Death (UK, US), directed by Leto Meade and Jonathan Rockefeller. A Special Mention went to Daughters of the Late Colonel (UK, Germany), directed by Elizabeth Hobbs.

The Student Film Award went to To Kill a Velofahrer (Switzerland), directed by Helmi Korhonen, Ines Nungässer, Livio Frauendorf and Marvin Büeler. A Special Mention was awarded to Land of No Man (US, Taiwan), directed by Muling Tzai and Olivia Lin. The Immersive Film Award was presented to Mirage (Bangladesh, Netherlands, Saudi Arabia), directed by Naima Karim. The Commissioned Film Award went to Kikkoman: Unleash Legendary (US), directed by Mariano Fernández Russo of Clubcamping. A Special Mention was awarded to Should Have Gone to Specsavers: Garbologist (UK), directed by Sammy Lewis. The Children’s Award went to Singularity (Netherlands), directed by Andy Goralczyk. Special Mentions were awarded to Grounded (New Zealand), directed by Chris Cullus, and Into the Forest (Switzerland), directed by Antonin Niclass, with Into the Forest going on to win the Audience Award.

The Industry Excellence Awards recognise outstanding creative talent and achievement across the animation industry, celebrating excellence in scriptwriting, storyboarding, character animation and character design. The Scriptwriting Award went to Joe Wells for Pablo Next Level (BBC, RTÉ, Crayola Studios), with Bryony James receiving the Storyboarding Award for the same production. Sam Turner took home the Character Animation award for Do I Look Like I Care? (Genentech), while Kostas Firinidis was recognised for Character Design for How Smart are Crows? (TED-Ed).

The festival also celebrated three films as part of its MAFter Dark programme, showcasing distinctive and unconventional animated work from international filmmakers. The selection includes Andrew Ganvickton (UK), directed by Joseph Pelling; Wuthering Hearts (UK), directed by Laura Jayne Hodkin; and Gone Wrong (France), directed by Anne-Linh Jérôme, Ambre Butel, Roman Saunier, Maxime Arnould, Juliette Houël, Adrian Villeda, Alisson Colombe and Ylan Dinguidar.

The Festival, which ran from 8-12 November at HOME and venues across Manchester, marked its biggest and most ambitious edition to date, bringing together audiences, filmmakers, artists and studios from across the globe for five days of screenings, premieres, studio showcases, masterclasses and behind-the-scenes events. The 2026 programme featured major studio presentations, exclusive previews and world-class talent, alongside headline events including the world premiere of Mog’s Bad Thing, Channel 4’s new adaptation of Judith Kerr’s beloved picture book, the UK premiere of Xilam’s LUCY LOST and a special preview screening of Warner Bros. pictures Animation and DNEG Animation’s The Cat in the Hat.

This year’s festival welcomed its largest audience to date, with almost 12,000 admissions across the five-day event. Delegate numbers were also at a high and projected to increase by a total of 10% once MAF Online concludes, with the curated digital programme extending the festival experience beyond Manchester. Together, these figures further cement Manchester Animation Festival’s position as one of the world’s leading animation events.

Manchester Animation Festival is presented with the support of Higher Education Partner University of Salford, Festival Partner HOME, Industry Supporter Manchester City Council, and Festival Patrons BBC Children’s, Blue Zoo Animation Studio, Channel 4, DNEG, Epic Games, Industrial Light & Magic, Manchester Metropolitan University, Nottingham Trent University, Sue Terry Voices and Universal Pictures. Original headline: Manchester Animation Festival Bans Generative AI Films for 2027 as 2026 Short Film Winners Revealed
English normalization: Manchester Animation Festival Bans Generative AI Films for 2027 as 2026 Short Film Winners Revealed
Full article body: Article too long to read?

The Oscar- and BAFTA-qualifying UK animation festival introduces stricter rules on generative AI as Georgian short When the Sea Was Calm and British animation A Little Death take major awards.

The Manchester Animation Festival (MAF) has announced that films containing generative-AI-created or transformed moving images will no longer be eligible for its competition from 2027, introducing a significant change to its submission policy as entries open for next year’s edition.

The announcement comes alongside the festival’s 2026 awards results, with Mamuka Tkeshelashvili’s When the Sea Was Calm winning the Short Film Award and Leto Meade and Jonathan Rockefeller’s A Little Death receiving Best British Short Film.

The 12th edition concluded on 12 November 2026, following five days of screenings, industry events and animation-focused discussions across Manchester.

The festival’s revised policy reflects a wider debate within the animation industry about generative AI, artistic ownership and the future of human-led creative production.

Manchester Animation Festival Introduces New Generative AI Restrictions

Under its newly published 2027 rules, Manchester Animation Festival will reject films if any part of the final moving image has been generated or transformed using a generative audio, image or video model.

The policy applies to films submitted to the festival’s competition from 2027 onwards.

The organizer also states that submissions found to be ineligible because of generative AI use will not necessarily be reviewed and will not qualify for a submission-fee refund.

This represents a more restrictive approach than simply asking filmmakers to disclose their use of AI tools.

Importantly, the published rule specifically addresses generative content or transformation within the final moving image. It should not automatically be interpreted as a prohibition on every form of AI-assisted production workflow.

Filmmakers using automated tools during development or post-production should consult the festival’s full policy before submitting, particularly where the distinction between conventional software assistance and generative transformation may be unclear.

Festival Director Emphasizes Human Creativity

Festival director Dr Steve Henderson linked the change to the organization’s commitment to the artists and craftspeople working within animation.

He said the festival wanted its new rules to reflect support for the creative professionals whose skills underpin the medium.

The position follows earlier public comments from Henderson expressing concerns about how generative AI systems draw upon existing artistic work and the potential consequences for animation professionals.

The new policy makes those concerns part of the festival’s formal competition eligibility requirements.

As generative video tools become increasingly sophisticated, animation festivals face questions about how to assess artistic authorship, technical innovation and the use of machine-generated images.

Manchester’s decision establishes a clear position for its 2027 competition, although the practical interpretation of individual production techniques may require further guidance.

When the Sea Was Calm Wins the Oscar-Qualifying Short Film Award

The festival’s principal Short Film Award went to When the Sea Was Calm, directed by Georgian filmmaker Mamuka Tkeshelashvili.

The 18-minute animated short is set in Sokhumi in the summer of 1992, before the outbreak of war transforms its residents’ lives.

The story follows a 13-year-old boy experiencing his first love while spending his days cycling, swimming and playing football with friends.

When the conflict reaches the city, the girl he has fallen for is forced to leave.

Decades later, the boy, now an elderly man, returns to the ruined city, confronting the memories of a childhood interrupted by violence.

Using puppet and cut-out animation, Tkeshelashvili explores displacement, memory and the relationship between personal loss and historical conflict.

Caucasian Film Service and 20 Steps Productions produced the film, with Vladimer Katcharava credited as producer.

Its festival history includes appearances at Annecy and DOK Leipzig.

The Manchester Short Film Award is particularly significant because the festival qualifies films for the Academy Awards.

Under the festival’s published qualification rules, a Short Film Award recipient can be considered for the Academy Awards’ short-film competition without the standard theatrical qualifying run, provided the film meets the Academy’s remaining requirements.

The Manchester win does not earn an Oscar nomination, but it offers a potential route to Academy Awards consideration.

British filmmaker Anna Ginsburg’s Hag received a Special Mention in the Short Film competition.

A Little Death Takes Best British Short Film

A Little Death, co-directed by Leto Meade and Jonathan Rockefeller, won the Best British Short Film Award.

The 12-minute, 23-second UK–US animated production follows Death as he tries to train a gentle, easily distracted apprentice.

What should be a straightforward assignment becomes increasingly complicated as the apprentice struggles to follow Death’s methods.

Eventually, Death receives unexpected professional advice from the very person they have arrived to collect.

Adapted from Nicholas Gurewitch’s graphic novel Notes on a Case of Melancholia, Or: A Little Death, the short combines dark humor with a story about kindness, responsibility, and learning to approach familiar tasks differently.

Michelle Brøndum and Jonathan Rockefeller produced the film, with a screenplay by Rockefeller, cinematography by Jamie Touche, editing by Giorgia Zarantonello, and music by Alastair McNamara.

The cast includes John Sparkes and Nami Annette Gillet.

Its Manchester award follows a festival journey that has included selection at the 2026 Annecy International Animation Film Festival.

Elizabeth Hobbs’s Daughters of the Late Colonel, a UK–Germany production, received a Special Mention in the British Short Film category.

Swiss Animation Wins Student Film Award

The Student Film Award went to To Kill a Velofahrer, directed by Helmi Korhonen, Ines Nungässer, Livio Frauendorf and Marvin Büeler.

The Swiss animated comedy follows Franz, an urban planner defending his supposedly visionary bicycle-lane designs to his superiors.

Outside the meeting room, those plans create chaos across the city.

Running about three minutes and 20 seconds, the film was produced through the animation program at Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts, with SRF also involved in the production.

Its recognition demonstrates the role of student animation in the festival’s program.

Muling Tzai and Olivia Lin’s Land of No Man received a Special Mention.

Other Manchester Animation Festival 2026 Winners

The festival recognized work across international features, shorts, commissioned productions, immersive experiences, and children’s animation.

| Award | Winner | Director |

|---|---|---|

| Short Film | When the Sea Was Calm | Mamuka Tkeshelashvili |

| Best British Short | A Little Death | Leto Meade, Jonathan Rockefeller |

| Student Film | To Kill a Velofahrer | Helmi Korhonen, Ines Nungässer, Livio Frauendorf, Marvin Büeler |

| Feature Film | In Waves | Phuong Mai Nguyen |

| Immersive Film | Mirage | Naima Karim |

| Commissioned Film | Kikkoman: Unleash Legendary | Mariano Fernández Russo |

| Children’s Award | Singularity | Andy Goralczyk |

| Audience Award | Into the Forest | Antonin Niclass |

The Industry Excellence Awards also recognized individual contributions to writing, storyboarding, character animation, and character design.

Joe Wells received the Scriptwriting Award for Pablo Next Level, while Bryony James won Storyboarding for the same production.

Sam Turner received the Character Animation Award for Do I Look Like I Care?, and Kostas Firinidis was recognized for Character Design on How Smart Are Crows?

The awards highlight a range of animation disciplines, including the creative and technical roles that contribute to completed productions.

What the AI Policy Means for Filmmakers

For animators considering future festival submissions, the new rule adds an important eligibility consideration.

Generative AI is already being used within some filmmaking workflows for image creation, video generation, visual transformation, and other production tasks.

Manchester’s policy distinguishes between animation created through human-directed artistic processes and final moving-image content generated or transformed by generative models.

The decision could influence how filmmakers document their production methods and select festivals for their work.

It also raises broader questions for the animation industry about the relationship between technology and authorship.

Some filmmakers view generative tools as a way to experiment with visual ideas or reduce production costs. Others argue that their use raises unresolved concerns about consent, training data, creative employment and the protection of artistic work.

Manchester Animation Festival’s revised rules clearly align its competition with the latter concerns about creative ownership and craft.

However, the long-term consequences for submissions, festival programming and the wider animation sector remain to be seen.

Manchester Animation Festival 2027 Submissions Are Open

Submissions for the next edition opened on 12 November 2026, and the festival is scheduled to return 14–18 November 2027.

The 2027 FilmFreeway listing provides the following deadlines:

| Stage | Date |

|---|---|

| Submissions opened | 12 November 2026 |

| Early-bird deadline | 3 March 2027 |

| Regular deadline | 23 June 2027 |

| Final deadline | 30 July 2027 |

| Selection notification | 10 September 2027 |

| Festival | 14–18 November 2027 |

Short films must run under 30 minutes and have been completed after 17 July 2026.

Filmmakers may enter works in progress, provided they clearly identify their status and deliver the completed film by 27 August 2027.

The published early-bird standard fee is £15 for short films and £7.50 for student films, with higher fees applying at later submission stages.

Filmmakers must review the revised generative AI requirements before submitting.

Applications are available through the festival’s official FilmFreeway page.

What Happens Next?

The 2026 competition has concluded, with the winning films continuing their respective festival journeys and potential awards campaigns.

For When the Sea Was Calm, the Manchester Short Film Award creates an Academy Awards qualification opportunity, subject to the Academy’s rules.

For filmmakers preparing new animated shorts, the immediate development is the opening of the 2027 submission cycle and its revised eligibility conditions.

As other festivals develop their own approaches to generative AI, Manchester’s decision may join a wider discussion about how international animation competitions define and recognize artistic authorship.

Full article body: The biggest betrayal this week—aside from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s against his wife, his mistress(es), company, country, and stock market—was… probably not the revelation that Big Walk’s developers made minor use of generative AI in the final stretch of the game’s development. But it still felt really bad! It’s hard not to look around the industry and come to the conclusion that this is just How Things Are Now, that AI is inescapable. But that doesn’t mean the battle is lost, nor that it was never worth fighting in the first place. On the latest Aftermath Hours, we discuss.

This time around, we convene to talk about the (at the time of recording) looming prospect of Jensen Huang’s complete career implosion brought on by—as could happen to any of us—his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. What happens to Nvidia now? And, I suppose more pressingly, what does this mean for the global economy, of which Nvidia props up a significant portion? Also, why do billionaires keep taking such unnecessary midlife crisis risks? Is it because they usually end up getting away with it? (Yeah.)

Then we move on to the other major headline of the week: As it turns out, Big Walk, an indie darling whose creators have taken a number of otherwise-progressive stances, was made with a tiny bit of help from generative AI. Why did this feel like such a betrayal to so many, despite AI not generating any in-game assets? And what does this mean for an industry where AI has begun to feel increasingly inescapable? Lastly, we talk about our various near-death experiences (spoiler: we survived them).

You can find this week's episode below and on Spotify, Apple, or wherever else you prefer to listen to podcasts. You can also watch it on YouTube. If you like what you hear, leave a review (or sub to our YouTube channel) so that we can someday spiral into a series of massively damaging midlife crises and destroy the United States economy once and for all.

Here’s an excerpt from our conversation (edited for length and clarity):

Nathan: I’ve seen a lot of people saying, “You’ve just gotta accept this; AI will be present in game development from now on.” And they’ll add that you’re taking an absolute stance against AI, but you’re doing it on Bluesky, which has been coded with AI, or you search on Google, which automatically pops up an AI module. You’re using it in that sense. You don’t have a choice, but you’re doing it.

So to, at this point, in the general progression of things, take an anti-AI stance in an absolute fashion, you’re fighting a losing battle. You’re swimming against the current, and you are ultimately not going to be able to accomplish anything. And I think that is a stupid and in its own way absolute stance in a few ways.

First, you don’t take a stance just because that’s the winning team. You don’t have principles because you think you’re on the side that’s for sure gonna come out on top in the end. You have principles to have principles. And, yes, in some cases it’s impossible to avoid AI. That doesn’t mean you should immediately give up, shrug your shoulders, and completely roll over. You fight battles where you can.

Luke: It’s “We live in a society.”

Nathan: Right, it’s like that meme of “Yet you participate in society? Curious!” Like, yeah, because there’s nothing else to participate in. I can participate in society or starve to death.

Then there’s the other element of—and Riley mentioned this, too—the internet having been hollowed out and destroyed in large part by AI companies or companies that have come to embrace AI like Google. That’s definitely a cause of the problem Big Walk’s developers encountered. But I think that in using AI to solve the problem, you are also contributing to a future even-more-hollowed-out internet.

You’re basically conceding that ground to AI instead of saying, “OK well, if there’s not this functional and searchable ecosystem of blogs and websites or good Unity documentation or what have you, we’ve gotta help rebuild or reassemble it.” And yes, I’m aware that Big Walk’s developers sought out assistance from other people and did what they could to some degree.

But I think once you decide to throw up your hands and use a chatbot, if everyone starts doing that, then there will no longer be an impetus to build the other, better alternative thing. It’s just gonna be people using AI. And that’s what the AI companies want. It’s why they hollowed out the internet in the first place and allowed it to become so corroded.

Full article body: 科技近在眼前 苏州首批人工智能终端产品集合店授牌

在近日举行的2026江苏人工智能创新发展大会暨第二届人工智能OPC大会上，苏州首批六家人工智能终端产品集合店授牌。

走进位于相城区的全国具身智能机器人和低空航空器展销中心，这里不仅有会跳芭蕾、练武术的机器人，各类低空航空器也一应俱全。

作为此次授牌的首批人工智能终端产品集合店，这里不仅为市民提供场景体验，还是商家产品展销及相关产业生态服务的集合地。作为入驻企业，宏途创联为各类具身智能企业提供平台研发、本体适配等服务。

北京宏途创联科技有限公司江苏区域总监郭盛表示，自主研发建设并运营了具身智能综合管控平台，场景覆盖矿业、化工、能源等领域，能够适配多种类型机器人，支持跨品牌的统一接入及集群表演，把工业现场真实案例转换为可视化的展示和实训场景。

据了解，全国具身智能机器人和低空航空器展销中心面积达1.2万平方米，已吸引人形机器人、四足机器人等相关领域的企业入驻。

苏州市低空运营服务有限公司副总经理朱云飞表示，聚焦低空经济和具身智能机器人两大前沿领域，包括宇树科技、云深处科技等人形机器人头部企业，目前展馆二期工程已启动建设，在一期展示互动竞赛基础上进一步扩容升级，未来这里不只是参观体验的空间，更会升级成为具身智能实训基地、赛事举办中心和产业对接平台。

包含全国具身智能机器人和低空航空器展销中心在内，苏州首批人工智能终端产品集合店还包括全球首家机器人6S店昆山店等6家，均于今年开业，具备集中展示、互动体验和常态化运营能力。
